#106141. Tech Report: As COP31 Antalya kicks off, can world move beyond major promises?

Tech Report: As COP31 Antalya kicks off, can world move beyond major promises?

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya's marketing video is clear: Turkey, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.
  • Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkey's first lady calling climate change "one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet.".
  • According to recent reports, from November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya's marketing video is clear: Turkey, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.

Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkey's first lady calling climate change "one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet.".

According to recent reports, from November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis. Turkey is the official host, and Australia will lead the negotiations. But the challenges they'll confront during those 12 days are far more serious than the showy marketing campaign make them out to be.

Severe drought, extreme heat, wildfires and record-low water levels in Europe's main waterways — summer across the continent was dominated by climate emergencies.

Sources indicate that and in late August, a series of flash floods triggered by a rock-ice avalanche in Nepal and Tibet washed away entire villages, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands missing. Climate experts have linked the disaster to melting ice and a warming climate.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Globally, carbon emissions are still rising: the UN has concluded that it is no longer possible to keep global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, the goal agreed at COP21 in 2015.

Recent findings suggest that the global transition away from polluting fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas will be at the center of attention in Antalya — once again. To date, there's been no consensus on whether and how to transition rapidly away from this main source of global warming.

Despite the setbacks, the world has made some progress thanks to the 2015 Paris Agreement.

David Victor, a climate expert at the University of California San Diego, pointed out that before then, the planet was hurtling toward an average temperature rise of between 3-3.5 C.

If current climate commitments are fully implemented, the latest UN projections show a rise of up to 2.6 C. It's a significant step forward, even though warming of that magnitude will still have worldwide consequences.

"There's no question that we could be doing more," said Victor, though he cautioned against pinning too much on this year's summit.

According to recent reports, all agreements at COP need to be unanimous, meaning individual states can quash any sweeping resolutions. Added to that challenge are the ongoing wars, trade conflicts and other economic problems swirling around this year's negotiations.

"It's like a giant Christmas tree in which everybody's hung their different ornaments, and the tree is groaning and more ornaments are being put on it," said Victor. "We have to look at it for what it is: It's a place where people talk about stuff.".

Instead of waiting for all COP member states to agree, Victor sees a better chance for change in what he called "clubs" — smaller alliances of governments and companies working together to advance actual solutions, whether it be in aviation, shipping or electromobility.

"The Paris process is important. It has to go forward," he told DW. "But all the work is going to be done in clubs.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

An example of this approach was last April's first ever International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia.

Colombia and the Netherlands invited representatives from 57 countries and key sectors to discuss ways to move the world away from coal, oil and gas, after an agreement on a similar plan failed at the 2025 climate summit due to opposition from several oil-producing states.

With an eye to the ongoing trade conflicts and energy crisis, hosts Turkey and Australia have included green industrialization and the clean energy transition among their aims. One goal is to increase the share of electricity in global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from around 20% today.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A recent analysis by the International Energy Agency found accelerating electrification could cut fuel-importing countries' energy bills by more than $400 billion (€357 billion) by 2035, compared to 2025 levels. The idea could appeal to regions dependent on fossil fuel imports — among them Germany and the European Union.

Ahead of COP31, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said Germany and the EU wanted to spark new momentum in the "global phaseout of fossil fuels.".

It's wouldn't just be good for the climate, but a chance for many countries to boost their economies and reduce dependence on energy imports, added Schneider in a statement.

Sources indicate that oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia, however, aren't interested in deals that will undermine their business model. At recent UN climate conferences, they've repeatedly blocked any final agreements, including phaseout looks.

In a recent development, even China, despite its massive expansion of wind and solar energy over the last 20 years, could be against the idea. The economic superpower traditionally rejects any outside demands, proposals or interference concerning its national decisions on energy policy.

Every country in the world is affected by climate change, with loss and damage calculated in the hundreds of billions from heat, drought and storms. Worst hit are vulnerable countries in the Global South and island nations, who are at risk of disappearing as sea levels rise.

That's where money comes into play, with developing countries calling for more support to protect their citizens from the harms of global warming. At the 2024 UN climate talks in Baku, Azerbaijan, industrialized nations agreed to free up at least $300 billion annually in climate financing by 2035.

Industry observers note that but where exactly all those funds will come from remains hotly debated. At the same time, several major developed countries — most notably, the US — have cut their development aid.

The German government only paid out €4.7 billion from its 2025 budget for international climate financing, down from €6.1 billion in 2024.

"The level of financial support for developing countries today is far from what's needed," mentioned Jan Kowalzig, a climate expert at Oxfam Germany.

Breaking financial promises like this comes at the expense of losing the trust of developing countries and, as a result, the diplomatic power which Germany and other industrialized nations rely on to shape policy to fight climate change.

Cosima Cassel, who focuses on climate diplomacy at the independent think tank E3G in Berlin, believes Turkey's push to turbocharge electrification during an oil crisis could be successful.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

For Cassel, a successful outcome at what are expected to be difficult negotiations in Antalya would reveal actual political will behind the grand agreements.

When it comes to electrification, that means taking the expansion of electricity grids and battery storage capacity seriously — not to mention removing the barriers to further electrification.

This article was originally written in German.

Juventus and Torino the only Serie A sides without a penalty either way after 11 rounds

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (524 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Juvefc

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that eleven rounds into the Serie A season, Juventus have neither won nor conceded a penalty, a distinction shared only with Torino.
  • It has been revealed that juventus have reached the November break without a single penalty decision in their league matches.
  • That makes Juventus an outlier, even in a season of fewer spot-kicks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that eleven rounds into the Serie A season, Juventus have neither won nor conceded a penalty, a distinction shared only with Torino. With the league's penalty rate down and the team seventh, the João Mario handball in Florence has become the clearest example of a call that went against them.

It has been revealed that juventus have reached the November break without a single penalty decision in their league matches. Seven sides are still waiting for a penalty in their favour: Roma, Juventus, Torino, Lecce, Fiorentina, Sassuolo and Udinese. Seven have yet to concede one: Inter, Milan, Como, Juventus, Napoli, Torino and Genoa. Only the two Turin clubs appear on both lists.

That makes Juventus an outlier, even in a season of fewer spot-kicks. Sportmediaset puts the number of teams still waiting for a penalty partly down to the latest refereeing approach introduced by Orsato.

It has been revealed that the wider numbers show a quieter season from the spot. The 24 penalties so far work out at about 0.22 per match, compared with 0.28 and 0.27 in the two previous seasons. The drop was sharpest early on. Only five of the 24 penalties came in the first five rounds.

The trend has not been flat since then. The rate rose to 0.31 per match after the September international break. Juventus have not shared in that rise. Their total in both columns remains zero.

The contrast with last season is clear. Juventus were awarded five league penalties then. They also had the last three saved: David’s against Lecce, Yildiz’s against Cremonese and Locatelli’s against Sassuolo.

According to recent reports, the case that has drawn most attention came late in the 2-2 draw at Fiorentina. João Mario handled the ball. No penalty was given. Gianluca Rocchi, who now works as a DAZN pundit, remarked it should have been a spot-kick. His reasoning was that the arm was out wide and the player had time to move it, even though the ball came from a teammate.

Luciano Spalletti signalled that he also saw a penalty. He chose not to complain publicly about the decision.

According to recent reports, close calls carry weight at this stage. Juventus are seventh on 18 points, six behind fourth place. Champions League qualification is in doubt. An injury-hit squad cannot easily absorb lost points from decisions at the margins.

Recent findings suggest that the run after the break will test whether the pattern holds. Venezia, the next league opponents, are among five clubs to have conceded three penalties, the league’s highest total. Frosinone, Bologna, Atalanta and Sassuolo share that figure. Sassuolo are also on the list of sides yet to be awarded one.

In a recent development, the schedule is crowded. After Venezia, Juventus host Omonia in the Europa League. A league trip to Como follows, then Sassuolo at home in the Coppa Italia. Como have yet to concede a penalty this season.

The first of those fixtures has already moved. Lega Serie A brought Juventus v Venezia forward to Sunday 22 November at 12:30, from its original slot on Monday 23 November at 20:45.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Joel Lefevre | 25 Nov 2026 14:36.

Real Salt Lake will try to extend their season into next week with a Friday win over the Vancouver Whitecaps at America First Field in game two of that best-of-three playoff series.

The reigning MLS Cup runners-up captured game one 2-0 last Sunday, putting them one win away from round two in the Western Conference playoffs.

After surviving a nervy shootout in the Wild Card Round, Salt Lake are now on the brink of elimination yet again after a subpar showing in game one against the Caps.

On Sunday, Pablo Mastroeni’s men suffered just their second defeat in their last eight MLS outings and were second-best for much of the game.

While they are on the verge of another early exit, they can draw optimism from being unbeaten in their last four MLS affairs at America First Field.

During the regular season, Salt Lake highlighted strong attacking potency on home soil, netting three or more goals six times and scoring multiple times on 12 separate occasions.

They will try to end a five-match playoff losing run on Friday, scoring a goal or fewer in each of those instances.

Claret and Cobalt have not lost a playoff match at home in 90 minutes this decade, with their only such victory at America First Field occurring on penalties versus the Houston Dynamo in game two of that opening round series.

It is just one game, but Vancouver looked very much like title contenders as they began the 2026 MLS post-season in style.

Jesper Sorensen’s side carried the play throughout game one and will seek a fifth consecutive MLS triumph on Friday.

While this is the fourth straight year the Caps are in the post-season, they have won only once in that span in normal time away from home, beating San Diego 3-1 in the Western Conference Final last year.

Meanwhile, they failed to win three of their final four regular-season away fixtures this season against Western Conference opposition, with the highest-scoring team in the West failing to score on two of those occasions.

Vancouver have never lost a playoff encounter under Sorensen when netting first but have also never won a post-season outing in 90 minutes when conceding the opener under his leadership.

Sorensen, meanwhile, has won every match against RSL as the Caps boss, including their last two visits to America First Field, in which his team scored three goals both times.

Real Salt Lake Major League Soccer form:.

Vancouver Whitecaps Major League Soccer form:.

Due to a hamstring strain, Ariath Piol may miss this match for RSL, while Diego Luna and Emeka Eneli are questionable because of knee injuries and Zach Booth still has to clear concussion protocol.

Sergi Solans has scored three goals in his last two MLS home outings, including the opener in their 2-1 win over the Los Angeles Galaxy on Decision Day, while Rafael Cabral kept game one close, making six saves, many of them spectacular.

On the Vancouver side, an illness may keep Belal Halbouni out on Friday, and it is unlikely we will see Kenji Cabrera feature as he deals with a foot injury.

Edier Ocampo got the Caps on the board late in the opening half of game one, with Bruno Caicedo adding some insurance in the final 45 minutes.

Real Salt Lake possible starting lineup:.

Cabral; Yedlin, Glad, Quinton, Engel, Sanabria; Lobjanidze, Guske, Spierings, Guilavogui; Solans.

Vancouver Whitecaps possible starting lineup:.

Takaoka; Ocampo, Blackmon, Priso, Johnson; Larraz, Cubas; Sabbi, Muller, Caicedo; White.

The Caps have far too many weapons for RSL to contend with, and even a heroic Cabral between the sticks might not be enough to fend off the visitors given their current form.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER.
  • Published: 12:00 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 12:16 EST, 24 November 2026.
  • As if having his first training session as Manchester United head coach sabotaged by a drone wasn’t dramatic enough, Mauricio Pochettino’s second day at work saw access to the club’s training base blocked by a serious road accident.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 12:00 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 12:16 EST, 24 November 2026.

As if having his first training session as Manchester United head coach sabotaged by a drone wasn’t dramatic enough, Mauricio Pochettino’s second day at work saw access to the club’s training base blocked by a serious road accident.

The collision between a vehicle and a cyclist on one of the two approaches to Carrington, where United’s players and staff are regularly seen driving through a security checkpoint, meant it was closed off for several hours on Friday while an ambulance and police cars attended the scene.

Greater Manchester Police say the cyclist was taken to hospital to receive treatment for injuries that were not life-threatening and no arrests were made.

However, anyone leaving Carrington had to take an alternative route in the opposite direction. That included the players after training and Pochettino and his staff following his first pre-match press conference.

The accident on Friday completed an eventful 48 hours at Carrington after a rogue drone operator filmed 12 minutes of Pochettino’s first training session and posted it on YouTube. He later took the video down and apologised for the intrusion, which United sources said was the right thing to do – even though they had not contacted the uploader directly and do not intend to take legal action against him.

They insisted there was not a breach of security at Carrington, but claimed a number of laws had been broken. Insiders promised a robust response to any further incidents to protect the rights of the club and its staff, and warned that those responsible would be ‘exposing themselves to significant legal and financial risk’.

It's been a testing first few days for Mauricio Pochettino as Manchester United boss.

One of the unexpected issues to hamper the Argentine was a drone filming his first training session.

Meanwhile, players leaving Carrington last Friday had to take an alternative route after a serious road accident near United's training ground.

Early start after Anfield mauling.

Confidential understands Pochettino ordered the United players into Carrington an hour early on Monday morning to flush the Liverpool defeat out of their systems as soon as possible.

The squad were pictured arriving around 8.30am as they looked to regroup after the 4-0 hammering at Anfield and begin their preparations for the Champions League tie against Sporting Lisbon in Portugal on Wednesday night.

The Argentine is eager to spend as much time as possible with the players on the training ground, having only taken over as United boss last Wednesday – four days before the Liverpool clash.

United now face 11 games in 43 days and sources believe there may not be too many days off as Pochettino tries to haul his team out of the relegation zone and ensure qualification for the knockout stage of the Champions League.

At least the indications are that he will allow the players to stay at home the night before games at Old Trafford, rather than having them cooped up in a hotel like some previous United managers.

Pochettino ordered the United players into Carrington an hour early on Monday morning to flush the Liverpool defeat out of their systems.

Matheus Cunha won’t play any part against Sporting following his red card in United's last Champions League tie against Roma three weeks ago.

Confidential has learned the Brazilian was set to claim the player of the match award after scoring two late goals in the 3-2 win over Roma, only for UEFA to step in.

UEFA rules prevent a player who has been sent off from receiving the award and so the selector – in this case Steve Cooper, the former Leicester, Nottingham Forest and Swansea boss who is now one of the governing body's technical observers – was forced into a late switch, picking Bruno Fernandes instead.

It has been revealed that cunha’s absence will be keenly felt in Portugal. He played no part in Tuesday’s training session at Carrington, instead working on his own in the gym.

At a time when United have the most porous defence in Europe’s top five leagues and Matthijs de Ligt, Leny Yoro, Lisandro Martinez and Ayden Heaven are all struggling for form, Pochettino is going to need Harry Maguire.

Pochettino overlooked the experienced Englishman from the start for the trip to Anfield but ended the match with Maguire on the pitch and he was United’s best defender on another desperate afternoon.

Maguire is walking the tightrope of a ban as he remains on four yellow cards after 11 league games. Players are hit with a one-match ban once they receive five or more yellows prior to the conclusion of the 19th league game of the season – eight matches from now.

Even after Yoro's red card at Anfield was overturned on appeal, Pochettino can ill-afford to be without Maguire going forward.

Pochettino is going to need the experience of Harry Maguire to hold his defence together but he faces a ban if he is booked again.

United are still waiting to see if Pochettino’s strength and conditioning specialist Silvia Tuya can join his staff at Carrington despite hiring fresh fitness coach Sam Wilson.

Wilson has joined United following his departure from Parma in October, having only moved to the Italian club as head of performance in the summer after 12 years at Arsenal.

It is understood Tuya has not yet been confirmed as part of Pochettino’s backroom team because she is waiting to see if a work permit will be approved.

She joined the US national team staff in October 2024 shortly after Pochettino, and travelled with him, first-team coach Miguel D’Agostino and analyst Alec Scott when they flew from Cincinnati to Manchester by private jet last week.

Strength and conditioning specialist Silvia Tuya has not yet been confirmed as part of Pochettino’s backroom team.

According to recent reports, some of the early changes under Pochettino have been more subtle than others. Observant fans may have noticed that when the club unveiled the team to face Liverpool at 3.15pm on Sunday, it was in positional order.

Previously, United’s line-up has been listed numerically, leaving fans to deliberate over the formation. But Pochettino liked to name his team positionally at Tottenham and Chelsea, and admitted in a Q&A on MUTV last week that he wants to do the same at United.

It was clear from the club’s social media post on Sunday that Pochettino would be sticking to the 4-3-2-1 formation favoured by Michael Carrick, with Patrick Dorgu returning on the left wing and Cunha leading the attack.

Not that it lasted very long, as Pochettino admitted he was forced to put his game plan ‘in the bin’ inside eight minutes when Yoro was sent off.

This weekend’s match-up between United and Brentford brings together the most ill-disciplined English team in all competitions and the dirtiest team in the Premier League.

No English team has had more players sent off this season than United’s four – Yoro twice, Cunha against Roma and Martinez against Chelsea.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Brentford are bottom of the Premier League’s disciplinary 'points table' thanks to their three red cards and 22 yellow cards. So expect referee Rob Jones to be a busy man on Pochettino’s home debut.

Leny Yoro brings down Alexander Isak at Anfield and is sent off - his second red card of the season.

Richard Arnold, who preceded Omar Berrada as United's chief executive, pocketed a £5.53m pay-off to stand down after Ineos moved into the club.

While Omar Berrada found himself back in the firing line last weekend, the man he succeeded as United’s chief executive was cutting a much more relaxed figure.

Richard Arnold, who led United between February 2022 and December 2023, was spotted enjoying himself on Chester’s popular Eastgate Street on Saturday night – 24 hours before a beleaguered Berrada watched United’s 4-0 thrashing 30 miles down the road at Anfield.

After stepping up to replace Ed Woodward, Arnold was in charge of United for the period spanning United’s strategic review which led to Sir Jim Ratcliffe acquiring 29 per cent of the club. Once it became clear that Ineos would take over the day-to-day running of United, he accepted a £5.53million pay-off to stand down, with the club’s general counsel Patrick Stewart stepping in on an interim basis.

Arnold is now enjoying a quieter life as an executive director at Norton Motorcycles and, it would appear, nights out close to his home near Chester.

It has been revealed that it was there that he met a group of United protesters outside his local pub in June 2022 and admitted that the last 12 months had been ‘a f****** nightmare’ and United had ‘f****** burned through cash’. Nothing much seems to have changed since then.

'Never Again!': Holocaust remembrance under pressure

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other.
  • In a recent development, "Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years.
  • In a recent development, wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other. "In a sense, they're trophies to post on social media for them to boast about — breaking the ultimate taboo," Jens-Christian Wagner, director of the Buchenwald and Mittelbau-Dora Memorials Foundation, told DW.

In a recent development, "Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years. We have seen memorial trees planted in honor of concentration camp victims cut down. When something like this happens — and it happens regularly — I find it particularly despicable because, because it ultimately kills these people a second time," added Wagner.

In a recent development, wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in Bonn's Bundeskunsthalle, or the Art and Exhibition Hall of the Federal Republic of Germany. Wagner remarked Holocaust remembrance is under pressure, and the subject of intensifying attacks.

Critics have dismissed remembrance as a "cult of guilt" or "national masochism." With right-wing populism on the rise and historical revisionism becoming more common, Wagner worries about how Germany will remember the victims murdered by the Nazi regime. He is also concerned about the future of democracy. And soon, there will be no Holocaust survivors left to tell the true story of what happened.

This new exhibition tackles this concern head-on with numerous works of art and historical artifacts.

Industry observers note that "I hope that perhaps even some people who don't already believe it's notable to confront Nazi crimes will find their way to the exhibition," Wagner stated. Memorial sites also attract visitors who aren't necessarily convinced of the need to confront these parts of history. Many of them are students.

"Let's not kid ourselves: When a teacher notes 'We're going there,' it's always a mandatory visit," he said.

For today's young people, the Nazi era seems like the distant past, Wagner explained. "When you tell them to remember something that their grandparents didn't even experience, it naturally feels like an emotional burden. They can practically see the finger being wagged at them, and that doesn't exactly encourage learning.".

In a recent development, A two-hour lecture won't have much of an impact if pupils aren't even paying attention. Instead, Buchenwald organizes full-day programs that allow students to explore historical sources together and make sense of history for themselves.

Industry observers note that the next step, Wagner said, is to show young people that this chapter of history isn't closed. Visitors are encouraged to make connections between the past and current events like migration, for example.

According to recent reports, "For the longest time, people have been discussing migration almost exclusively in terms of threats to public safety and crime. This broadly marginalizes certain groups — a mechanism that also worked for National Socialism," he stated.

In a recent development, eva Umlauf, 83, knows firsthand what it means to experience exclusion in its most extreme form. She is a patron of the Bonn exhibition.

In a recent development, in November 1944, Umlauf was just 2 years old when she, her pregnant mother and her father were deported by the Nazis from the Novaky labor camp in Slovakia to Auschwitz-Birkenau, the notorious Nazi concentration and extermination camp. She was saved from the gas chambers by mere days; the Nazis stopped using the chambers as the Red Army advanced, hoping to hide evidence of their crimes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The camp was liberated on January 27, 1945. Three months later, Umlauf's sister Nora was born. But her father, her mother's siblings and her grandparents were all murdered. Eva barely survived herself. She suffered from tuberculosis, rickets and whooping cough, as well as edema caused by starvation. "Forget about the child. She won't survive," a doctor told her mother. But he was wrong.

Her mother returned to what was then Czechoslovakia with her two daughters, settling in Trencin. Eva Umlauf has no conscious memories of Auschwitz, but she carries her family's trauma deep within her.

According to recent reports, her mother never talked about what happened. Even so, Eva knew from an early age that she was a survivor. Her family rarely mentioned the camp by name, but one sentence came up again and again: "They stayed there." Eva knew that meant "they" were dead. And then, there was the number tattooed onto her arm: A26959.

Sources indicate that her mother taught her daughters not to draw attention to their Jewish identity — antisemitism was widespread throughout Czechoslovakia at the time. The small family managed to avoid harassment.

According to recent reports, eva Umlauf wanted to become a pediatrician, so she studied medicine. In the 1960s, she met her future husband, Jakob, who had also survived the Holocaust. He was an architect, active in Munich's Jewish community. They married in 1966, and she moved to Germany. She could hardly have imagined that she would one day live in the country of the perpetrators. "I don't hate Germans," she said. "But I cannot forgive. How can you forgive the deaths of 6 million people?".

It wasn't until much later that she first spoke publicly about the horrors of her early childhood. In 2011, she delivered a commemorative speech in Auschwitz on the anniversary of the camp's liberation. Since 2025, she has served as chair of the International Auschwitz Committee. A heart attack in 2014 motivated her to write her first book. "I was in intensive care. I thought to myself: If I get out of here healthy, I'll write a book.".

According to recent reports, her memoir, "The Number on Your Forearm is Blue Like Your Eyes," was first released in 2016. The English translation followed in 2024. Since its publication, hardly a day has passed without someone asking Eva Umlauf to share her story.

It has been revealed that she is appalled by the disrespectful behavior of young people at former concentration camps and by growing ignorance about the Holocaust. Sometimes, people even ask if she's too old to have a tattoo. But she also recalls a young man on the Munich subway who noticed the number on her arm and told her: "I want to apologize to you for what my ancestors did to you.".

Umlauf never imagined that antisemitism would once again become so widespread in Europe and the United States. Nor did she expect the rise of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

Industry observers note that "I go into schools. I'm so overwhelmed by the number of requests asking for my availability. And yet, the AfD is growing faster than I can reach students. It makes me think all this work is for nothing," she told DW.

It has been revealed that germany must never again fall under a right-wing dictatorship, she stressed. "'Never again' sounds nice, but all I can say is: It's happening again! Wouldn't 'Here We Go Again: Never Again' make a good title for the exhibition?".

She also shared her message to young people in the exhibition catalog, "Never Again": "You are not responsible for the crimes of your grandparents and great-grandparents. But you are responsible for the future. […] You are the generation that will shape our world. Make it a place where everyone can grow up safely, regardless of their background, faith or skin color.".

In a recent development, she continues: "You don't have to be perfect. You just have to stay alert. Take care of your country.".

The exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn runs through May 2, 2027.

This article was originally written in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Adeyeye Oluwapelumi | 25 Nov 2026 16:48.

Maritimo and Nacional renew their Madeira derby rivalry in the Primeira Liga on Friday evening, with both sides looking to claim an crucial victory and move further clear of the drop zone.

The two clubs are meeting in the top flight for the first time in five years, with the visitors sitting 13th in the Primeira Liga table on 10 points from 11 matches, just two points above the 15th-placed hosts, who have a game in hand against Estoril Praia and sit outside the relegation playoff place on head-to-head points ahead of Casa Pia.

Maritimo made an encouraging start to life back in the top flight, winning their opening two league fixtures against Casa Pia and Famalicao, but they have not claimed another Primeira Liga victory since beating the latter on August 16.

Mitchell van der Gaag's side have since gone eight league matches without a win (D2, L6), including defeats in their last three such outings against Porto (2-1), Vitoria de Guimaraes (5-0) and Santa Clara (2-0).

Only bottom-placed Estoril, who are yet to win a league match this season, have endured a longer winless run, while Maritimo have scored the third-fewest goals in the division (nine) and conceded the third-most (21).

Van der Gaag's men have also struggled to make home advantage count, recording just one victory from five league matches at their own ground and losing the last three, during which they conceded multiple goals on each occasion and scored just once.

Maritimo did, however, receive a welcome boost in the Taca de Portugal last weekend, progressing past Chaves following a goalless draw and a 3-2 penalty shootout victory, and will hope that result provides some momentum ahead of Friday's derby.

Nacional have also endured a difficult start to the campaign, but they have collected six points from their last three matches, including a 1-0 victory over Academico de Viseu courtesy of Matchoi Djalo's late winner.

That result marked the first victory under new boss Joao Henriques, who arrived in late October as the club's third permanent manager of the season following the departures of Joao Giao and Alexandre Santos.

Henriques initially struggled to build on interim coach Bruno Abreu's home victory over Braga, losing away to Arouca in his first match in charge, but the latest success has given the Alvinegros an opportunity to record consecutive competitive wins for the first time since beating Alverca and Tondela in April.

Interestingly, Nacional's last four matches have each produced just one goal, including their disappointing Taca de Portugal defeat to lower-division Sanjoanense on October 17, meaning taking maximum points on Friday could hinge on greater efficiency in attack and defensive discipline.

However, the Islanders still have plenty of room for improvement away from home, having collected just one point from five Primeira Liga trips this season, drawing at Santa Clara on the opening weekend before losing their next four against Vitoria, Sporting, Rio Ave and Arouca.

Nacional have also found this fixture difficult in recent meetings, losing four of their last five league encounters with Maritimo across the Primeira Liga and Liga 2 (D1), including a 3-1 defeat on their most recent competitive visit.

Nacional form (all competitions):.

Maritimo are monitoring defenders Rafael Fernandes (muscle) and Paulo Henrique (thigh), who both missed last weekend's cup tie against Chaves.

Yellu Santiago is also working his way back to full fitness from an injury, having only featured in the opening weekend of the Primeira Liga campaign.

Goncal Tabuaco's performance against Chaves has given Van der Gaag a decision to make in goal after he replaced Fran Vieites in the cup, saving two penalties during the shootout.

Nacional will be without Ulisses Wilson and Filipe Soares, who are both recovering from ankle injuries and remain unavailable.

Leo Santos (knee) is also sidelined, while Brazilian duo Wesley Gasolina and Liziero continue to recover from their respective injuries.

Henriques could retain the lineup that started against Viseu, with Miguel Baeza anchoring the midfield, although Djalo is pushing for a starting place after making an impact from the bench last time out.

Maritimo possible starting lineup:.

Vieites; Igor Juliao, Correia, Szalai; Tavares, Andrade, Guzzo, Ogbeta; Bassouamina, Butzke Tejon.

Nacional possible starting lineup:.

Marin; Jensen, Goncalves, Vitor, Kokolo; Baeza, Dias, Djalo; Labidi, Njoya, Song.

Maritimo have struggled to turn home advantage into league points this season, but Nacional's poor away record gives the hosts reason to believe they can avoid defeat, making a share of the spoils a reasonable prediction.

  • The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Sources indicate that nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It noted in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.".

"The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the firm mentioned Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information.".

The organization's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

Recent findings suggest that "He's an honorable guy," remarked Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine.".

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he remarked.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this.".

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research tech giant Radio Free Mobile, said the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he mentioned.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the manufacturer is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO.".

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

In a recent development, however, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

Recent findings suggest that however, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

It has been revealed that windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the firm. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he mentioned.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion manufacturer in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

According to recent reports, what if Kylian Mbappé joined Liverpool after his adventure at Real Madrid? In any case, this is the conviction of Youssouf Mulumbu, former Paris Saint-Germain midfielder, who spoke about the future of the French striker in an interview with GOAL. While the Blues captain is still playing for Madrid, Mulumbu believes that a departure for the Premier League could be the next step in his career. “ I really think that after Real Madrid, if he wants to leave this club, and it’s a substantial “if” because he will stay there for a long time, he will go to Liverpool, for sure “, he noted. The former Parisian therefore does not believe in a return of Mbappé to PSG, in particular because of the circumstances of his departure in 2024. “ It’s ironic because the way he left PSG wasn’t the best “, he recalled. To justify his prediction, Mulumbu relies above all on the links already established between the French international and the Reds. “ He spoke with Jürgen Klopp at the time and he is a real Liverpool fan. It would be the best option for him and for the club “, he added. A hypothesis which, however, remains very distant, with no departure from Real Madrid currently being confirmed.

Recent findings suggest that this possibility did not come completely out of nowhere, since Kylian Mbappé himself admitted to having been close to joining Liverpool when he was still playing at AS Monaco. In an interview given to The Athletic last September, the French striker recounted the discussions initiated with Jürgen Klopp and his mother’s particular interest in the English club. “ Yes, I was close to Liverpool. My mother was a substantial admirer of Jürgen Klopp and Liverpool was her favorite destination “, he confided. Fayza Lamari even went to Anfield to discover the facilities and meet the managers, before falling under the spell of the club. Mbappé also revealed that he met Klopp during a particularly original exchange, on board a plane, during which the German coach presented his project to him. “ I told him: ‘You don’t need to convince me. You are Jürgen Klopp, this is Liverpool, a great club’ “, said the Frenchman. Despite these discussions, he ultimately favored PSG in order to win in his hometown. Now based at Real Madrid, where he is pursuing his goal of winning the Champions League and the Ballon d’Or, Mbappé therefore maintains a special history with Liverpool, even if there is no evidence today to confirm that he will one day join the Reds.

#106128. Structural basis of RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CAST systems

Structural basis of RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CAST systems

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 70 min read (13926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~70 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) achieve site-specific DNA integration by combining the RNA-guided targeting action of a nuclease-deficient CRISPR–Cas system with the assembly of a Tn7-like transpososome complex1,2.
  • Transposons are pervasive DNA segments capable of mobilizing within and between genomes, thus serving as potent drivers of genome evolution and horizontal gene transfer10,11,12.
  • The inherent programmability of CASTs has driven their development as genome-editing tools that enable the site-specific insertion of multi-kilobase DNA cargoes without generating double-stranded breaks in the target DNA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) achieve site-specific DNA integration by combining the RNA-guided targeting action of a nuclease-deficient CRISPR–Cas system with the assembly of a Tn7-like transpososome complex1,2. Understanding the detailed mechanisms of this elaborate process is paramount to engineering CAST systems into programmable genetic tools3,4,5,6. Type I-F Pseudoalteromonas CAST (PseCAST) shows the highest activity in mammalian cells so far7 and has been adapted extensively through directed evolution8. However, its continued rational engineering requires addressing critical gaps in our understanding of transpososome assembly and activation9. Here we perform structural analyses using cryogenic electron microscopy, validated by DNA transposition assays, to visualize the PseCAST system in a series of functional states that define the stepwise mechanism of RNA-guided DNA integration. The structures of the PseCAST targeting and transposase recruitment complexes revealed that conformational changes in the Cascade–TniQ module, induced by R-loop formation, are associated with target-DNA stabilization and TnsC heptamerization. This, in turn, results in the recruitment of the TnsAB transposase by conserved interactions with the carboxy-terminal tail of TnsB. Finally, the structure of the 1.2 MDa PseCAST transpososome holocomplex revealed allosteric coupling of TnsC–TnsB and TnsB–target-DNA interactions to the conformational remodelling of the TnsB catalytic site, activating donor-DNA integration. Together, these findings establish a unified mechanistic blueprint for RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CASTs and provide a structural framework to guide their engineering for genome-editing applications.

Transposons are pervasive DNA segments capable of mobilizing within and between genomes, thus serving as potent drivers of genome evolution and horizontal gene transfer10,11,12. CASTs have evolved repeatedly by exaptation of minimal, nuclease-deficient CRISPR–Cas systems to enable RNA-guided, site-specific DNA integration13,14,15. These systems operate through the concerted action of a CRISPR-based targeting module and a Tn7-like transposition machinery comprising the TnsC AAA+ ATPase, the TnsB transposase and, in some systems, the TnsA endonuclease. The CASTs characterized so far differ mainly in the organization of their DNA-targeting and transposition modules1,2,16,17,18. Type I variants typically use a multi-subunit Cascade–TniQ (QCascade) complex for target recognition guided by CRISPR RNA (crRNA) and TnsA–TnsB for cut-and-paste transposition19,20,21. By contrast, type V-K systems rely on the Cas12k–TniQ–S15 complex for crRNA-guided targeting5 and use only TnsB for copy-and-paste transposition, resulting in cointegrate products22. TnsC plays a pivotal part in all CASTs, acting as an adapter that bridges the targeting module and the transposase enzymes to define the insertion site23,24.

The inherent programmability of CASTs has driven their development as genome-editing tools that enable the site-specific insertion of multi-kilobase DNA cargoes without generating double-stranded breaks in the target DNA. CAST-based editing has been implemented in bacteria25,26,27,28 and mammalian cells7,8,29,30, offering considerable potential for research and therapeutic applications. Type V-K CASTs generally show low integration efficiencies in human cell lines29,30, limited specificity2,26,27,31 and heterogeneous insertion profiles22,30. By contrast, type I-F systems can perform precise, simple insertions with substantially higher efficiencies1,7,22,26. In particular, the type I-F system of the Pseudoalteromonas Tn7016 transposon (Fig. 1a) has emerged as a highly promising candidate for genome-engineering applications, because of its uniquely high integration activity in human cells7,9. Directed evolution and structure-guided engineering of PseCAST components in Escherichia coli have resulted in the evoCAST system. This system has markedly improved integration efficiencies, reaching up to 10–30% in human cells, yet maintains precise, cointegrate-free insertion outcomes8. Although structural studies of type V-K CAST systems have provided mechanistic insights into various stages of transpososome assembly5,6,32,33,34,35,36, structural information about type I CASTs is currently limited to sub-complexes9,19,20,21,37,38,39,40,41,42. This presents a knowledge gap in the mechanistic understanding of the RNA-guided DNA-integration pathway. Specifically, the mechanism by which the RNA-guided targeting module induces the assembly and catalytic activation of the transposase components remains unclear.

Recent findings suggest that a, Locus organization of the type I-F CAST of Pseudoalteromonas sp. S983 (Tn7016). RE, right transposon end; LE, left transposon end. b, Cryo-EM density map of the PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC targeting complex bound to DNA, coloured as in a. c, Atomic model of the PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC complex, coloured as in b. d, Schematic of the PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC complex, highlighting individual subunits. e, DNA organization in the targeting complex (left), with an accompanying diagram summarizing strand identity and protein footprints derived from the model (right). TGS, target strand; NTGS, non-target strand. f–h, Magnifications of the interactions between TniQ.1, TnsC.1 and TnsC.7, highlighting hydrophobic (f) and ionic (g) contacts as well as bridging interactions of TniQ.1 with the TnsC.1–TnsC.7 interface (h). i, Normalized transposition activity in E. coli of PseCAST containing mutations in the TniQ–TnsC interface, as determined by quantitative PCR (qPCR). j–l, Magnifications of the interaction interface between Cas8 and TnsC.5, highlighting electrostatic (j), polar (k) and aromatic (l) contacts. m, Normalized transposition activity in E. coli of PseCAST with mutations in the Cas8–TnsC interface, as determined by qPCR. i,m, Data are mean ± s.d. of three independent biological replicates (n = 3; circles); the catalytically inactive mutant TnsB(D220A) serves as a negative control.

Here we report a series of structural snapshots of the PseCAST system obtained using cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), including a previously unresolved transpososome holocomplex assembly comprising all molecular components. These snapshots reveal the molecular determinants and critical checkpoints at key stages of the RNA-guided DNA-integration pathway, including target DNA recognition, TnsC oligomerization, transposase recruitment and catalytic activation. Our findings define the molecular mechanisms that govern RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CASTs, thereby establishing a structural foundation for the further development of these systems as genome-engineering tools.

Industry observers note that tnsC oligomers function as bridging modules for the assembly of the transposition machinery in both type V-K and type I-B CASTs, interacting with the RNA-guided CRISPR module through their amino-terminal face and with the transposase through their carboxy-terminal face6,20,36,41. To elucidate the structural basis of the guide-RNA-dependent assembly of TnsC in the type I-F PseCAST, our initial cryo-EM analysis yielded a reconstruction of a target-DNA-bound complex comprising PseCascade–TniQ and a heptameric TnsC ring (hereafter the targeting complex) at an overall resolution of 3.1 Å (Fig. 1b–d, Extended Data Table 1 and Extended Data Fig. 1a–c). Resembling the architecture of TnsC heptamers from the canonical Tn7 element of E. coli and other type I CAST systems20,40,42,43 (Extended Data Fig. 2), the TnsC heptamer has a near-perfect seven-fold symmetry without a helical rise or seam, fully enclosing the DNA duplex in a positively charged central channel, in which all seven TnsC ATPase sites are occupied by ATP molecules and Mg2+ ions. The enclosed DNA adopts B-form geometry and is contacted by the Glu105–Asp120 loops of TnsC.1 and TnsC.5 through nonspecific interactions.

It has been revealed that notably, the structure of the targeting complex includes a complete 32-base-pair R-loop (Fig. 1e), which was only partially formed in the previously reported intermediate PseQCascade complex structure9. In contrast to the open arrangement of the partial R-loop intermediate9, the Cas8 α-helical bundle (residues 272–421) undergoes an approximately 90° rotation into a closed or locked state (Extended Data Fig. 3a), establishing additional contacts with the protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM)-distal segment of the target DNA, both TniQ subunits and Cas7.5 (Extended Data Fig. 3b–d). Moreover, three nucleotides of the displaced non-target strand (NTGS) are bound in a pocket in the Cas8 bundle (Extended Data Fig. 3e), which likely facilitates reannealing of the NTGS with the target strand (TGS) in the PAM-distal DNA segment and its interactions with the TniQ dimer. This feature is absent from the partial R-loop and open helical-bundle states of type I-F CAST QCascade complexes published previously19,21. As the presence of a full R-loop and a closed Cas8 helical-bundle conformation have been suggested to be a prerequisite for stable target engagement21, our structural observations indicate that the formation of the locked state serves as a target fidelity checkpoint upstream of transposase recruitment.

Unexpectedly, the structure of the PseCAST targeting complex revealed that the TnsC heptamer interacts with both TniQ.1 and Cas8 through extensive interfaces spanning 947 Å2 and 818 Å2, respectively (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 3f), forming a ‘super-ring’ assembly that bridges the PAM-proximal and PAM-distal ends of the QCascade subcomplex. At the N-terminal face of the heptamer, TnsC protomers use the same surfaces for interactions with both TniQ and Cas8 (Extended Data Fig. 3f). At the PAM-distal end, the N-terminal region of TniQ.1 is wedged into the TnsC.1–TnsC.7 inter-subunit interface. An aromatic pocket in TniQ.1 comprising Phe3, Phe5, Phe29 and Phe30 interacts with a hydrophobic loop in TnsC.1 containing Leu101, Leu104, Leu106, Phe107 and Ile112 (Fig. 1f). TnsC.1 further engages TniQ.1 in a series of ionic interactions (Fig. 1g) and bridging interactions that also contact the TnsC.1–TnsC.7 interface (Fig. 1h). Individual mutations in the inserted TnsC loop (L106S or F107A) did not affect the transposition activity of PseCAST in E. coli. By contrast, a strong synergistic effect in the TnsC double mutant L106A, F107A led to a near-complete loss of transposition activity (Fig. 1i). Whereas alanine substitutions in pairs of residues in the TniQ hydrophobic pocket (either F3A and F5A, or F29A and F30A) had a mild effect on transposition efficiency (Fig. 1i), charge-reversal substitutions at these positions (either F3E and F5E, or F29E and F30E) had a substantially stronger effect (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Deletion of the seven N-terminal TniQ residues resulted in the loss of transposition activity (Fig. 1i). Moreover, cross-subunit mutant combinations involving residues in the TnsC loop and the TniQ hydrophobic pocket, either TnsC(L106S) and TniQ(F3A, F5A), or TnsC(F107A) and TniQ(F29A, F30A), resulted in a marked decrease in or the complete loss of transposition activity in vivo (Fig. 1i), confirming the importance of the TniQ–TnsC interactions for the assembly of the PseCAST transpososome.

At the PAM-proximal end, Cas8 and TnsC.5 form a shape-complementary interface, mediated by aromatic and electrostatic interactions (Fig. 1j–l). The combination of TnsC mutations R68A, Y75A, R77A and Pheresulted in a pronounced reduction in transposition activity in vivo (Fig. 1m), indicating that the Cas8–TnsC interaction contributes to transpososome assembly. However, mutations of interacting residues in Cas8, alone or in cross-subunit combinations with TnsC, had a mild or negligible effect (Fig. 1m), suggesting that the sensitivity of the TnsC–Cas8 interface to mutational perturbations is lower than that of the TnsC–TniQ interface. Similarly, whereas the individual charge-reversal TnsC mutant Y75E alone was sufficient to decrease transposition activity substantially, single charge-reversal mutations in Cas8 (T486R, W465E or H469E) had variable effects on transposition efficiency (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Together, these structural observations define the molecular coupling between the CRISPR targeting machinery and TnsC that results in the assembly of an ATP-loaded TnsC heptamer on the target DNA.

It has been revealed that in the canonical Tn7 element in E. coli44, as well as in the type V-K CAST system of Scytonema hofmanni (ShCAST) and the type I-B CAST system of Peltigera membranacea cyanobiont 210A (PmcCAST), transposase recruitment is mediated by TnsC interactions with the C-terminal region of TnsB6,23,41. In the structure of the paired-end complex (PEC) of PseTnsAB, the C-terminal tail of PseTnsB (residues 574–613) is disordered45. To assess whether the unstructured tail plays a similar part in interacting with PseTnsC, we performed co-precipitation experiments using affinity-tagged PseTnsB constructs comprising either the full-length protein or the standalone C-terminal tail (TnsB(575–613)) (Fig. 2a). Both full-length TnsB and TnsB(575–613) co-precipitated target-DNA-bound QCascade and TnsC efficiently in the presence of ATP (Fig. 2b), indicating that TnsB interacts directly with the targeting complex and that its C-terminal tail is sufficient for this interaction. The amount of co-precipitated TnsC remained unchanged in the presence of the non-hydrolysable ATP analogue ATPγS (Extended Data Fig. 4a), indicating that, similar to the type I-B PmcCAST system41,42, TnsB does not stimulate ATPase-dependent depolymerization of TnsC in PseCAST. Furthermore, co-precipitation of TnsC by TnsB(575–613) decreased strongly in the absence of ATP, suggesting that the interaction requires ATP-dependent TnsC oligomerization (Extended Data Fig. 4b). This result was corroborated by the loss of TnsC co-precipitation in the absence of QCascade or after introducing mutations in the TniQ- and Cas8-interacting interfaces (Extended Data Fig. 4c). Together, these results indicate that TnsB recruitment requires QCascade-dependent assembly of TnsC on the target DNA.

a, Domain organization of PseTnsA, PseTnsB and an artificial PseTnsAB fusion protein. Numbers above the schematic refer to amino-acid positions for individual proteins; numbers below refer to the PseTnsAB fusion protein. CAT, catalytic domain; C-tail, C-terminal tail; DBD1 and DBD2, DNA-binding domains 1 and 2, respectively; NLS, nuclear localization signal. The C-terminal hook motif (residues 605–613) is highlighted in yellow. b, Co-precipitation of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC targeting complex by amylose-immobilized His6–MBP-tagged full-length TnsB (left) or C-terminal tail (right) in the presence of ATP and target DNA. CQC, Cascade–TniQ–TnsC; I, 5% input control; E, elution. Representative results from two independent replicates are shown. For gel source data, see Supplementary Fig. 2. c, Cryo-EM density map of the PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC transposase recruitment complex bound to TnsB hook motifs. d, Atomic model of the PseCascade–TniQ–TnsC transposase recruitment complex bound to TnsB hook motifs. The seventh TnsB hook is located at the back of the structure and is not visible in this side view. e, Right, atomic model of the TnsB hook-decorated TnsC heptamer. Left, magnification of the interactions between TnsC.2 and the TnsB.2 hook motif. f, Normalized transposition activity in E. coli of PseCAST containing mutations in the TnsB hook, as determined by qPCR. Data are mean ± s.d. of three independent biological replicates (n = 3; circles); TnsB mutation D220A serves as a negative control.

To validate these findings structurally, we aimed to reconstitute and determine the structure of QCascade–TnsC in complex with TnsAB bound to the excised transposon ends. To this end, we performed affinity co-precipitation using a recombinant TnsAB fusion protein construct (Fig. 2a), pre-assembled with a segment of the right end of the transposon (RE), to capture the QCascade–TnsC complex assembled on the target substrate comprising a linear double-stranded DNA (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Single-particle cryo-EM analysis of the resulting sample yielded a 2.8-Å reconstruction of a PseCAST transposase recruitment complex comprising target-bound QCascade and heptamerized TnsC decorated with TnsB C-terminal segments (or TnsB hooks; residues Trp605–Glu613). The TnsB hooks are bound to all TnsC subunits at the junction between the N-terminal α/β core domain and the C-terminal α-helical bundle close to the ATP binding pocket (Fig. 2c,d, Extended Data Table 2 and Extended Data Fig. 5a–c), similar to the arrangement described for type V-K34,36 and I-B41,42 CASTs (Extended Data Fig. 6). They are anchored by hydrophobic interactions of TnsB residues Trp605, Leu609 and Phe612 and an additional hydrogen bond between the backbone carbonyl of residue Asp606 of TnsB and Arg212 of TnsC (Fig. 2e). Corroborating these observations, TnsB mutation W605A caused a substantial decrease in the transposition activity of PseCAST in E. coli. Moreover, individual TnsB mutations L609K or F612A, as well as the deletion of the entire TnsB hook (Δ604–613) resulted in a complete loss of transposition activity (Fig. 2f). These findings highlight the functional requirement of the interactions between the TnsB hook and TnsC for the transposition activity of PseCAST and demonstrate the critical role of the TnsB C-terminal tail in the recruitment of the TnsAB transposase and for the delivery of the transposon DNA to the target site before integration.

It has been revealed that to determine the structure of the PseCAST transpososome holocomplex comprising Cascade, TniQ, TnsC and TnsAB, we used a modified ‘one pot’ affinity co-precipitation strategy to trap the transpososome in a post-integration strand-transfer complex (STC) state (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 7), which has been used previously to visualize transpososome structures because of its stability6,34,36,41,46,47. The assembly used a minimal symmetrized RE donor sequence, which supports transposition in related systems48,49 and is sufficient for the formation of a paired-end PseTnsAB complex45. Cryo-EM analysis of the resulting sample, supported by three-dimensional variability analysis combined with heterogeneous and locally focused refinement, yielded a reconstruction with a global resolution of 3.1 Å (Fig. 3b, Extended Data Table 3 and Extended Data Fig. 8a–d). The reconstruction revealed that the transposase adopts an intertwined, pseudo-twofold arrangement with a TnsA2–TnsB4 stoichiometry to assemble on the structured DNA in an STC configuration (Fig. 3c,d). All seven TnsC subunits are bound to the C-terminal hook motifs of TnsAB (Fig. 3b,c); it is not possible to ascertain which of these are connected to the bound TnsAB or contributed by unbound TnsAB molecules in trans, as the connecting segments (residues 824–843) of TnsAB are unstructured. The target DNA exits from the central channel of the TnsC heptamer and extends towards the TnsAB tetramer assembled on the pseudo-palindromic target site duplication (TSD) region and the adjacent transposon end sequences (Fig. 3a). As in the structure of the TnsAB PEC45, each transposon end is occupied by two TnsB protomers: a proximal catalytic subunit (TnsB.1 or TnsB.2)—the catalytic domain of which engages the other transposon end in trans—and a distal structural subunit (TnsB.3 or TnsB.4) (Fig. 3c). Only two TnsA subunits (TnsA.1 and TnsA.2), bound to the catalytic TnsB protomers, are resolved in the structure. The corresponding interaction interfaces in the structural TnsB subunits are occupied by the bound RE DNA duplexes, precluding TnsA interactions.

Industry observers note that the structure of the PseCAST holocomplex reveals the molecular interactions responsible for the TnsC-dependent recruitment of TnsAB to the target DNA to effect site-specific donor integration. The TnsB.1 subunit is tethered to the C-terminal face of the TnsC heptamer by its β-barrel domain (residues 434–500), positioned at the interface of the TnsC.1 and TnsC.7 subunits (Fig. 3e). TnsC.1 inserts its C-terminal loop—spanning residues 314–322 and including Leu318—into a hydrophobic pocket formed by Val472, Gln467 and Leu441 in the TnsB.1 β-barrel domain (Fig. 3e). In turn, Asn316 of TnsC, situated in the same loop in TnsC.7, interacts through hydrogen bonds with Arg443 and Asn444 in TnsB.1 (Fig. 3e). Aspartate substitutions of Leu318 in TnsC (L318D) or Val472 in TnsB (V472D) resulted in a pronounced reduction in transposition activity in vivo (Fig. 3f). The single TnsC mutation N316A or replacement of TnsC loop residues 316–321 with a (Gly–Ser)3 linker resulted in modestly impaired activity. By contrast, the single TnsB mutations R443E or N444D strongly reduced transposition activity (Fig. 3f), confirming that the formation of this interface is essential for PseCAST-mediated DNA transposition.

According to recent reports, in addition to interactions with TnsC, the β-barrel domain of the catalytic TnsB.1 subunit also interacts with the backbone of the target DNA segment downstream of the TnsC heptamer, forming a network of hydrogen bonds and electrostatic contacts using Arg439, Thr440, Lys447 and Gln449 of TnsB (Fig. 3g). Furthermore, Lys520 and Arg524 in the C-terminal helical domain of TnsB also contact the target DNA backbone. Notably, this domain adopts a helical bundle fold that bridges the catalytic and β-barrel domains in the catalytic TnsB.1 and TnsB.2 subunits. By contrast, the helical domain of the structural TnsB.3 and TnsB.4 subunits forms two stretched helices that are sandwiched between the catalytic domain and DNA-binding domain 2 of TnsAB.1 and TnsAB.2, contributing to intra-subunit contacts.

It has been revealed that together, these insights highlight the functional role of the TnsB β-barrel domain in transpososome assembly. The shape complementarity of the TnsC and TnsB β-barrel interaction surfaces, together with cooperative interactions with the target DNA, provide the structural basis for the molecular ruler mechanism that defines the integration site, enabling the transposon to be inserted at a fixed distance of 49 nucleotides from the crRNA-specified target site. Moreover, the synergistic contacts with two TnsC subunits and the target DNA underlie a checkpoint mechanism that senses target DNA-dependent TnsC oligomerization, thereby explaining the strictly sequential assembly of the transpososome observed in type I-F systems40.

The structure of the PseCAST transpososome holocomplex captures the TnsAB STC tetramer in a post-integration state (Fig. 4a,b). As in the PEC structure45, the active sites of the TnsA.1 and TnsA.2 subunits interact with the 5′ termini of the transposon ends, adopting a catalytically competent, post-cleavage geometry in which the catalytic triad residues Glu34, Asp71 and Lys87 of TnsA coordinate the 5′-terminal phosphate group and a single Mg2+ ion (Fig. 4c). In contrast to the PEC structure, the catalytic sites of the TnsB.1 and TnsB.2 subunits also assume an activated conformation in which a Mg2+ ion—coordinated by the catalytic triad residues Asp220, Asp304 and Glu340 of TnsB—interacts with the 3′-hydroxyl group of the terminal nucleotide (dG76 in the NTGS) of the target DNA and the phosphodiester group that links the TSD segment to the 3′-terminal nucleotide of the transposon end (Fig. 4d). Furthermore, the catalytic domain establishes contacts with RE and TSD nucleotides that are crucial for STC formation (Fig. 4d). Specifically, Asp225 of TnsB positions an additional Mg2+ ion such that it simultaneously coordinates the phosphate groups of dA(−82) and dG(−80), stabilizing a kink in the DNA backbone at the TSD–RE junction that enables STC formation. The backbone is additionally contacted by Thr222, Arg239 and Ser360 of TnsB (Fig. 4d). Consistent with these observations, alanine substitution of Asp225 (D225A) or a charge-reversal mutation of Arg239 of TnsB (R239E) resulted in a complete loss of PseCAST transposition activity in E. coli, whereas TnsB mutations T222A or S360A only reduced PseCAST activity (Fig. 4e).
