It has been revealed that finally, the PseCAST transpososome holocomplex structure highlights a potential allosteric relay mechanism that underlies the target-DNA-dependent catalytic activation of TnsB. In the PEC structure, the β-barrel and C-terminal helical domains of the catalytic TnsB subunits are disordered45. By contrast, both domains are structured in the STC state and interface with the catalytic domain (Fig. 4b) through a network of hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions (Fig. 4f). This is coupled with local structural remodelling of the catalytic domain, resulting in the ordering of an adjacent loop (residues Glu348–Lys369 of TnsB) (Fig. 4g) and an approximately 11-Å concomitant shift of the helix bearing the catalytic Glu340 residue of TnsB (Fig. 4g). The conformational rearrangement marks the transition of the catalytic site from an inactive, post-excision state to an active, strand-transfer configuration that supports Mg2+ coordination and catalytic activity. Consistent with these observations, combined alanine substitutions of Lys567, Gln571 and Asn577 in the C-terminal helical domain of TnsB strongly reduced the transposition activity of PseCAST in E. coli (Fig. 4i). Additional ordering was observed for the N-terminal segment (residues Met1–Pro11) of the TnsA helical domain, which positions the Arg4 residue of TnsA such that it contacts the 5′-terminal phosphate of the cleaved transposon end (Fig. 4c,h), implicating TnsA in TnsB activation. Accordingly, truncation of the TnsA N-terminal segment (ΔMet1–Asn12) resulted in a complete loss of transposition activity (Fig. 4i). Together, the structural observations and their functional validation indicate that the molecular interfaces formed between the C-terminal, β-barrel and catalytic domains of TnsB after binding to the target DNA and TnsC are required to support the integration activity of PseCAST. Both target DNA and TnsC synergistically couple transposase recruitment with domain ordering and catalytic-site remodelling, resulting in the allosteric activation of TnsB for site-specific DNA integration.

Our structural and functional analyses of the PseCAST system comprehensively revealed the molecular mechanism that underlies RNA-guided transposon integration by type I-F CASTs, in which an orchestrated series of interactions and conformational rearrangements couples target recognition with site-specific DNA insertion. Together, these insights support a mechanistic model in which DNA transposition is controlled by a succession of molecular checkpoints (Fig. 5). The formation of the QCascade–TnsC targeting complex requires R-loop completion, enabled by a conformational rearrangement of the Cas8 subunit, including the approximately 90° rotation of the helical bundle domain into a locked conformation. In contrast to the open conformations reported previously for type I-F CAST QCascade complexes9,19,21,37, this locked state positions the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex for binding to TniQ, which facilitates ATP-dependent TnsC assembly on the target DNA by interacting with Cas8 and TniQ. As the locked Cas8 conformation is achieved only with fully matched targets, it acts as a fidelity checkpoint that discriminates against mismatched sites, underpinning the high target specificity of PseCAST. Instead of forming extended filaments as in type V CASTs32,33, PseTnsC assembles into a symmetric heptamer to fully encircle the DNA duplex exiting QCascade. The transposon insertion site is thus defined by the physical footprint and register of the TnsC ring, rather than by TnsB-dependent TnsC depolymerization6,32,33. The initial recruitment of the TnsAB transposase PEC is mediated by the TnsB C-terminal tail hook motifs. As these interactions are dependent on TnsC heptamerization, this step provides another fidelity checkpoint that makes transposition dependent on the correct recognition of the DNA target. Finally, productive target engagement by TnsAB requires conformational ordering of the TnsB β-barrel domain and C-terminal helices, driven by interactions of the TnsB β-barrel domain with the target DNA and the TnsC heptamer. This is coupled with structural remodelling of the TnsB active site into a catalytically competent configuration. Therefore, the TnsC- and target-DNA-dependent catalytic activation of TnsB acts as a final fidelity checkpoint, ensuring that transposon DNA insertion proceeds only once the transposase is correctly anchored to the target DNA. Together, our findings reveal the structural coupling of target DNA engagement and transposase activation, but the precise role of allosteric interactions in the observed conformational rearrangements requires further investigation. We speculate that similar structural coupling is involved in activating TnsAB for transposon excision after interacting with the flanking segments of the donor DNA.

The Cascade–TniQ complex is guided to the target DNA by base-pairing with its crRNA, leading to the initial formation of a partial R-loop. Coordination of the displaced NTGS by the Cas8 helical bundle is coupled with the transition of the bundle from open to closed, full R-loop formation and the stabilization of the double-stranded PAM-distal target-DNA duplex by the TniQ dimer. TnsC is recruited to the target site, where it assembles into a closed heptameric ring by binding to the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex in the presence of ATP, TniQ and Cas8. At the donor site, excision of the transposon DNA by TnsAB involves the formation of a PEC. The PEC is initially recruited by the TnsC heptamer by interacting with the C-terminal TnsB hooks. Interactions with the target DNA and TnsC result in structural remodelling of the β-barrel and C-terminal helical domains of the interfacing TnsB copies, which is allosterically coupled with a conformational rearrangement of the catalytic domains into an active conformation (the asterisks indicate active TnsB sites). The transposon DNA is integrated by two transesterification reactions catalysed by the active sites of the interfacing TnsBs, covalently linking both transposon 3′ ends to the target DNA with 5-base-pair spacing that results in a target-site duplication (TSD).

Industry observers note that directed evolution and structure-guided engineering are powerful complementary strategies for improving CAST activity8,9, recalling previous studies in which structural insights have enabled the rational design of hyperactive variants of the Sleeping Beauty transposase50,51. To provide a structural context for current engineering efforts, we mapped the activity-enhancing substitutions of evoCAST onto the PseCAST holocomplex structure (Extended Data Fig. 9). Two of these, F43S in TnsB and P88T in TnsA, have already been interpreted structurally in the PseTnsAB PEC as potentially facilitating transposon end recognition and stabilizing the cleaved NTGS overhang, respectively. Several of the remaining substitutions in TnsB, which were mostly unresolved in the PEC, can now be interpreted. Y349N, P352T and D396N are found close to the target-DNA substrate, potentially enhancing its binding. Q410K, V526E and Q549R are predominantly surface-facing and thus likely to enhance protein solubility or stability. Q594L, although unresolved in the holocomplex structure, may provide additional hydrophobic interactions to the interface formed between the C-terminal hook and TnsC, which is essential for transposase recruitment. Finally, H464R may promote the interaction between the TnsB β-barrel domain and TnsC through enhanced electrostatic contacts. The substitutions R197I and N314K in TnsC map to the TnsC oligomerization interface and the TnsC–TnsB interface, respectively. Lastly, in addition to the PAM-enhancing mutations N125D and A244N in Cas8, the A410R substitution in the helical bundle likely contacts the PAM-distal target-DNA duplex after R-loop completion (Fig. 5), potentially stabilizing the locked QCascade conformation and promoting TnsC assembly. Together, these insights suggest that evoCAST activity results from the synergistic optimization of DNA binding, intersubunit contacts, folding and solubility. Therefore, future engineering efforts should continue to use both structure-guided and directed-evolution approaches.

In conclusion, the structural findings presented here reveal the molecular mechanisms underpinning RNA-guided transposition by type I CASTs, providing a framework for their further rational engineering for technological applications.

Industry observers note that the expression plasmids containing His10–TEV-tagged TniQ and Cas8 (pSL4521), Cas7, Cas6 and the CRISPR array (pSL4522), His6–SUMO–TEV-tagged TnsC (pSL5536) and His6–SUMO–TEV-tagged TnsAB fusion protein (pSL3768) were cloned using standard molecular biology methods including Gibson52 and Golden Gate53 assembly. All plasmids were sequence-verified using whole-plasmid Nanopore sequencing (Genewiz). To clone the expression plasmid containing Cas7, the CRISPR array and Twin-Strep-tagged Cas6 (pMS321), a Twin-Strep-tag54 was added to the C-terminus of cas6 by Gibson assembly: pSL4522 was linearized by PCR using oMS603 and oMS604, and the Twin-Strep-tag was amplified by PCR from a common backbone using the primers oMS605 and oMS606, which contain overhangs compatible with the linearized pSL4522 plasmid. Constructs for expression of His6–MBP-tagged versions of the TnsAB fusion protein and TnsB were generated by PCR amplification of the coding sequence using pSL3768 as template and primer pairs oMS631-632 and oMS634-632, respectively. The PCR products were inserted in the 1C backbone (Addgene; 29654) by ligation-independent cloning55. The His6–MBP-tagged TnsB C-terminal tail (residues 575–613) was prepared by Gibson assembly, using the His6–MBP–TnsB plasmid as a template and the primer pairs oGF181-182 and oGF180-184 to generate the PCR fragments. Plasmids were cloned and propagated in Mach I cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific), purified using the GeneJET plasmid miniprep kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and verified by full-plasmid sequencing or Sanger sequencing (Microsynth). All sequences of primers and parental plasmids used for cloning are provided in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2.

In a recent development, for Cascade–TniQ protein expression, the plasmid pSL4521 encoding His10–TEV–TniQ and Cas8 and the plasmid pMS321 encoding Cas7, Cas6–Twin-Strep and the crRNA were transformed together in 50 μl of E. coli BL21 Rosetta2 (DE3) cells (Novagen), plated on an agar plate and incubated at 37 °C overnight. A single colony was inoculated in 100 ml of Luria broth (LB) to obtain a starter culture. Both the transformation plate and liquid medium were supplemented with 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin, 50 µg ml−1 streptomycin and 33 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol. After overnight growth at 37 °C and 220 rpm, the starter culture was added to eight 750-ml flasks containing antibiotic-supplemented (kanamycin, streptomycin) LB medium to reach a starting optical density at 600 nm (OD600) of 0.05. Cell cultures were grown at 37 °C with shaking at 110 rpm until an OD600 of 0.6 was reached. Protein expression was induced with 0.4 mM isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) for 16 h at 18 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation (4,000g at 4 °C for 30 min) and resuspended in 100 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin and 200 μg ml−1 4-(2-aminoethyl)benzenesulfonyl fluoride (AEBSF). The suspension was lysed using a Maximator cell homogenizer at 1,500 bar and 4 °C. The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000g at 4 °C for 40 min) and applied to three 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in lysis buffer. The columns were washed with 200 ml of HisTrap wash buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole) and eluted with 50 ml of HisTrap elution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 250 mM imidazole). Dithiothreitol (DTT) and ATP were added to the eluted sample to a final concentration of 1 mM each. The sample was added to 7 ml of 50% Strep-Tactin affinity resin suspension (IBA Lifesciences) in HisTrap elution buffer. The mixture was incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 30 min. The protein-bound resin was washed with 70 ml of size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 500 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT) and the sample was eluted with 20 ml of SEC buffer supplemented with 5 mM d-desthiobiotin. Eluted fractions were further purified by SEC using a Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL (Cytiva) column in SEC buffer. Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 10 mg ml−1 using a 30-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use.

For TnsC expression, the vector pSL5536 encoding His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsC was transformed in 50 μl of E. coli BL21 Star (DE3) cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific), plated on an agar plate supplemented with 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin and incubated at 37 °C overnight. A single colony was inoculated in 100 ml of kanamycin-supplemented LB to obtain a starter culture. After overnight growth at 37 °C and 220 rpm, the starter culture was added to eight 750-ml flasks containing kanamycin-supplemented LB medium to reach a starting OD600 of 0.05. Cell cultures were grown at 37 °C with shaking at 110 rpm until an OD600 of 0.6 was reached. Protein expression was induced with 0.3 mM IPTG for 16 h at 18 °C. Cells were collected by centrifugation (4,000g at 4 °C for 30 min). Proteins were purified as described previously for the TnsC of Vibrio cholerae40. A cell pellet (corresponding to four 750-ml liquid cultures) was resuspended in 40 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 5 mM magnesium acetate, 0.2 mM EDTA, 0.1% (v/v) Triton X-100, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin, 200 μg ml−1 AEBSF and 1 μg ml−1 DNase. The suspension was lysed by ultrasonication (Bandelin Sonopuls HD 3200 equipped with a VS 70 T probe, 1 s on–2 s off cycle, at 20% amplitude for 15 min at 4 °C). The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000 g at 4 °C for 45 min) and applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in equilibration buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 10 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT). The columns were washed with 90 ml of equilibration buffer and 50 ml of wash buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 30 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT), and the proteins were eluted with 10 ml of elution buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 5% (v/v) glycerol, 300 mM imidazole, 1 mM DTT). Elution fractions were pooled and dialysed overnight against 2 l of dialysis buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 1% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT, 10 mM imidazole) in the presence of 2% (w/w) His6-tagged TEV protease. Any precipitated protein was removed by centrifugation (20,000g at 4 °C for 20 min). The dialysed proteins were applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in equilibration buffer. The columns were washed with 60 ml of equilibration buffer, 90 ml of wash buffer and 50 ml of elution buffer. Flowthrough and initial wash fractions were applied to a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) equilibrated in SEC buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 0.2 mM EDTA, 1% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM DTT). Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 12 mg ml−1 using a 10-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use.

For the expression of His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsAB (pSL3768), His6–MBP–TEV–TnsAB (pMS329), His6–MBP–TEV–TnsB (pMS331) and His6–MBP–TEV–TnsB(575–613) (pGF189), the procedure described for His6–SUMO–TEV–TnsC was followed, except that 0.4 mM IPTG was used to induce protein expression instead of 0.3 mM. For the purification of untagged TnsAB, TnsB or TnsB(575–613), a cell pellet (corresponding to four 750 ml liquid cultures) was resuspended in 40 ml of lysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM imidazole, 5% glycerol) supplemented with 1 μg ml−1 pepstatin, 200 μg ml−1 AEBSF and 1 μg ml−1 DNase. The suspension was lysed by ultrasonication (Bandelin Sonopuls HD 3200 equipped with a VS 70 T probe, 1 s on–2 s off cycle, at 30% amplitude for 15 min at 4 °C). The lysate was cleared by centrifugation (40,000g at 4 °C for 1 h) and applied to two 5-ml HisTrap HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in lysis buffer. The columns were washed with 50 ml of lysis buffer, and the proteins were eluted in a stepwise gradient (5%, 20% and 100%) of elution buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole, 5% glycerol). Fractions corresponding to the 20% and 100% of elution-buffer concentrations were pooled and dialysed overnight in 2 l of dialysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol, 1 mM DTT) in the presence of 2% (w/w) His6-tagged TEV protease. Dialysed proteins were applied to two 5-ml HiTrap Heparin HP columns (Cytiva) connected in tandem and equilibrated in dialysis buffer, washed with 30 ml of dialysis buffer and eluted in a linear gradient of heparin buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 1 M NaCl, 5% glycerol, 1 mM DTT) over 150 ml (target concentration of heparin buffer: 100%). Peak fractions were pooled and further purified by SEC using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) equilibrated in SEC buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT). Purified proteins were concentrated to approximately 15 mg ml−1 using a 50-kDa molecular-mass cut-off centrifugal filter (Merck Millipore), flash frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until further use. For the expression and purification of His6–MBP-tagged TnsAB, TnsB and TnsB(575–613), the procedures described for untagged TnsAB, TnsB and TnsB(575–613), respectively, were followed, except that the TEV-cleavage and heparin steps were omitted.

It has been revealed that A double-stranded target DNA (dsTarget) was prepared by annealing the synthetic oligonucleotides oMS628 and oMS629 (Supplementary Table 3) in a 1:1 ratio at a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. The pull-down procedure involved mixing the assembly buffer (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 50 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT), 300 pmol of DNA substrate, water and 300 pmol of Cascade–TniQ and incubating this mixture at room temperature for 10 min. Subsequently, ATP or ATPγS (at 1 mM final concentration) was added to the sample, followed by 2,400 pmol of TnsC. The mixture was further incubated at room temperature for 30 min, after which 300 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsB(575–613) or full-length His6–MBP–TnsB was added to the sample to a final volume of 53 μl. After 30 min at room temperature, 147 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP or ATPγS) was added to the sample. Then, 10 μl were withdrawn and mixed with 10 μl of water and 5 μl of SDS dye (225 mM Tris-HCl pH 6.8, 50% (v/v) glycerol, 5% (w/v) SDS, 0.05% (w/v) bromophenol blue, 250 mM DTT) to obtain a 5% input control sample for SDS–PAGE analysis. The sample was mixed with 50 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer and incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1 h. After a short centrifugation (500g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. Subsequently, 25 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose was added to the sample. After centrifugation (14,000g at 4 °C for 2 min), 20 μl of supernatant was mixed with 5 μl of SDS dye to obtain an elution sample for SDS-PAGE analysis. Next, 10 μl of 5% input control and 10 μl of elution sample were loaded on a 10% SDS-PAGE gel (Bio-Rad) for each tested condition. For the control samples Cascade–TniQ–TnsC-minus or MBP–TnsB/AB-minus, the respective SEC buffers were used instead of a protein solution. SDS-PAGE gels were imaged using a ChemiDoc Imaging system (Image Lab Touch software v.4.1, Bio-Rad) and analysed using Image Lab (v.6.1.0, Bio-Rad).

A PseCAST pDonor plasmid was first transformed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells (NEB). Single colonies were inoculated in a liquid culture and the resulting strains were made chemically competent using standard methods. PseCAST pEffector plasmids encoding a crRNA targeting the lacZ locus (crRNA-4) and all CAST subunits were transformed in the resulting strain and plated on double-antibiotic LB agar plates containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin and 100 µg ml−1 spectinomycin. After approximately 20 h of growth, surviving colonies were scraped from the plates, resuspended in fresh LB medium and re-plated on double-antibiotic LB agar plates supplemented with 0.1 mM IPTG to induce PseCAST protein expression. Cells were incubated for an additional 18–20 h, scraped and resuspended in LB medium. Cells were then lysed and integration efficiencies were measured using qPCR as described previously1. Data were plotted and statistical analyses performed in GraphPad Prism (v.11.0.0, GraphPad). Wild-type plasmid sequences, crRNA-4 and oligonucleotides used for qPCR are listed in Supplementary Tables 1 and 2.

The cryo-EM reconstruction of the QCascade–TnsC targeting complex resulted from an initial attempt to reconstitute the QCascade–TnsC–TnsAB holocomplex. Target- and donor-DNA constructs were prepared by annealing the synthetic oligonucleotides oMS572, oMS573 and oMS576 (target; Supplementary Table 3) and oMS569, oMS570 and oMS571 (donor; Supplementary Table 3) at a 1:1:1 molar ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program involved incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. For the target pot assembly, 10× buffer (200 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 1,500 mM KCl, 100 mM MgCl2, 10 mM DTT), water and TniQ–Cascade were gently mixed on ice. The target DNA was added and the sample was incubated at room temperature for 10 min. TnsC and ATP were added to the sample, which was then incubated at room temperature for 15 min. The final target pot volume was 25 μl, containing 4.5 μM of Cascade–TniQ, 4.5 μM of target DNA, 40.5 μM of TnsC, 1 mM ATP, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2 and 1 mM DTT. The donor pot was prepared by mixing 10× buffer, water, ATP, TnsAB and donor DNA to a final volume of 25 μl (containing 18 μM TnsAB, 4.5 μM of donor DNA, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 150 mM KCl, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM ATP and 1 mM DTT) and then incubating the mixture at room temperature for 10 min. However, a white insoluble precipitation was observed in the donor pot at this stage and again after mixing with the target pot and incubating at room temperature for 20 min. This was likely due to TnsAB instability under the conditions used. In fact, the donor pot components were not detected in the subsequent cryo-EM analysis. After mixing the target and donor pots, the sample was centrifuged (14,000g at 4 °C for 10 min) and the pellet discarded. Next, 2.5 μl of supernatant was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (30 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 2 s (100% humidity, 4 °C) and plunge-frozen in liquid ethane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI), followed by storage in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on an FEI Titan Krios G3i system (University of Zurich, Switzerland) operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 9,403 movies were acquired at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 47 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 59.672 e− Å−2. EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

In total, 9,403 exposures were imported into cryoSPARC56 live (v.4.3) for real-time processing. After patch-motion and patch-CTF (contrast transfer function) correction, 745,080 particles were identified using blob picker (200–300 Å diameter), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 50 two-dimensional (2D) classes. Next, 416,193 particles were selected and three volumes were generated using ab initio reconstruction. One class yielded a recognizable Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume (108,814 particles) and was used for three-dimensional variability analysis (3DVA; filter resolution: 5 Å; mode: simple); the other two volumes did not contain density for TnsC. Two distinct volumes, resulting from one 3DVA mode, were used as input for heterogeneous refinement to separate the particles of Cascade–TniQ–TnsC from those of Cascade–TniQ only. The two volumes, after a round of non-uniform refinement, were used as inputs for a second heterogeneous refinement, together with one of the volumes from the ab initio multi-class round. This refinement resulted in a volume of Cascade (195,798 particles), Cascade–TniQ (143,494 particles) and Cascade–TniQ–TnsC (76,901 particles). The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume was used for non-uniform refinement after particle re-extraction (76,400 particles), yielding a reconstruction at a resolution of 3.07 Å, as calculated by gold-standard Fourier shell correlation (GSFSC). After particle subtraction, a local refinement of the TnsC heptamer generated a 3.44-Å (GSFSC resolution) map. A composite map was obtained by combining the consensus Cascade–TniQ–TnsC and TnsC-focused volumes using the combine_focused_maps function in Phenix57 (v.2.0-5936). Particles corresponding to Cascade only were used as an input for a 3DVA and heterogeneous refinement as described above. One of the resulting volumes, corresponding to 132,574 particles, yielded a 2.86-Å (GSFSC resolution) Cascade reconstruction after particle re-extraction and non-uniform refinement. The Cascade–TniQ volume was fed twice into a heterogeneous refinement. One of the volumes, corresponding to 50,074 particles, yielded a 3.19 Å (GSFSC resolution) reconstruction after particle re-extraction and non-uniform refinement. All maps and models have been deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) and Protein Data Bank (PDB) (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 1). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 1. Monomeric initial models of Cas6, Cas7, Cas8, TniQ and TnsC were generated using AlphaFold3 (ref. 58). The AlphaFold3 models were docked manually as rigid bodies in the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX59 (v.1.9). The model was real-space refined in Phenix (v.2.0-5936) against the cryo-EM map and then manually in Coot60 (v.0.9.4) using secondary structure, side chain rotamer, Ramachandran and LibG61 nucleic-acid restraints. The nucleic acid model, comprising the crRNA (positions −7 to 52), TGS (positions −60 to 4) and NTGS (positions −4 to 4, 21 to 23 and 34 to 60), was built manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using PDB accession 7U5D (ref. 21) as a starting point. The cryo-EM density was clear enough to distinguish the DNA register. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 1. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1, Adobe). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC complex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1a–f.

The cryo-EM sample of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsB hook recruitment complex was obtained using a pull-down approach. The dsTarget and a double-stranded right-end donor DNA (dsRE) were prepared by annealing synthetic oligonucleotides oMS628-629 and oMS576-630 (Supplementary Table 3), respectively, in a 1:1 ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM in annealing buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 100 mM KCl). The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. The target pot was prepared by adding 1,200 pmol of dsTarget to 100 μl of assembly buffer (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 2 mM DTT), after which KCl solution was added to a final KCl concentration of 230 mM and 1,200 pmol of Cascade–TniQ. The mixture was incubated at room temperature for 10 min, after which ATP and 8,400 pmol of TnsC were added. The sample was then incubated at room temperature for 30 min. The final target pot volume was 200 μl and its buffer composition was 1 mM ATP, 20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 1 mM DTT and 230 mM KCl. A donor pot was prepared by mixing 1,200 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsAB and 1,200 pmol of dsRE substrate. The donor pot was brought to a 20 μl final volume using TnsAB SEC buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 500 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT), mixed with the target pot and incubated at room temperature for 30 min. After adding 30 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP), the sample was mixed with 40 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer and incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1 h. After centrifugation (500 g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. Next, 15 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose was added and the sample was centrifuged (14,000 g at 4 °C for 5 min). The supernatant was isolated by careful pipetting and centrifuged two additional times. A second elution was performed using 20 μl of maltose-supplemented binding buffer, followed by three centrifugation steps as described above. The two eluates were combined into one sample and used to freeze cryo-EM grids. Two and a half microlitres of sample was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (60 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 2.5 s at 100% humidity and 4 °C, plunge-frozen in a cryogenic mixture of liquid ethane and propane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI) and stored in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on a FEI Titan Krios G3i system operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 11,374 movies were acquired at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 37 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 60.947 e− Å−2. EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

In a recent development, in total, 11,374 exposures were imported into cryoSPARC live (v.4.7) for real-time processing. After patch-motion and patch-CTF correction, 329,059 particles were identified using blob picker (200–300-Å diameter), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 50 2D classes. The selected 114,608 particles were used as a training set for Topaz picking (350-Å expected particle diameter, 50 particles per micrograph), yielding 463,242 particles, which were extracted (extraction box size: 500 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 250 pixels) and classified in 150 2D classes. Classes corresponding to 189,451 particles were selected and fed into a two-class ab initio reconstruction, resulting in a junk class and a recognizable Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume (142,343 particles), which was used as input for non-uniform refinement after particle re-extraction. A 2.84-Å (GSFSC resolution) reconstruction was obtained from a final number of 138,834 particles, which was further used for a TnsC-focused local refinement, yielding a 2.96-Å (GSFSC resolution) volume of the heptamer decorated with additional density for each of its seven subunits. A composite map was obtained combining the consensus Cascade–TniQ–TnsC and TnsC-focused volumes using the combine_focused_maps function in Phenix (v.2.0-5936). All maps and models have been deposited in the EMDB and PDB (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 2). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 5. The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC model was rigid-body fitted into the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and adjusted manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using the above-mentioned restraints. The DNA duplex was extended by three nucleotides at the 5′ end of the TGS and by two nucleotides at its 3′ end, with the NTGS extended correspondingly. An initial model of the TnsC heptamer bound to seven TnsB(575–613) copies was generated using AlphaFold3 and docked manually. The model placed the last nine TnsB C-terminal residues at the additional densities of each TnsC subunit. The recognizable density of the bulky TnsB residues Trp605 and Phe612 aided in fitting the TnsB hook in the density. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 2. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsB hook complex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1g–m.

It has been revealed that the cryo-EM sample of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsAB holocomplex was prepared using a pull-down approach. The strand-transfer substrate was prepared by annealing oligos oMS733, oMS734 and oSO146 (Supplementary Table 3) in a 1:1:1 ratio to a final concentration of 100 μM each. The annealing program consisted of incubation at 95 °C for 5 min, followed by a 1 °C min−1 rampdown until 12 °C was reached. Next, 1,000 pmol of substrate, 22.5 μl of assembly buffer A (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 200 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT) and water were mixed with 2,000 pmol of His6–MBP–TnsAB to a final volume of 45 μl, and the sample was kept on ice for 10 min. In the meantime, 35.8 μl (1,000 pmol) of Cascade–TniQ was mixed with 55 μl of assembly buffer B (40 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 20 mM MgCl2, 100 mM KCl, 2 mM DTT) and 1.6 μl of water to reduce its KCl concentration to 260 mM. This mixture was added to the initial pot and incubated at room temperature for 10 min. ATP (1 mM final concentration) was added, followed by 7,000 pmol of TnsC, reaching a final volume of 155 μl. The mixture was then incubated at room temperature for 30 min. After the addition of 45 μl of binding buffer (20 mM HEPES-KOH pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl2, 300 mM KCl, 1 mM DTT, 0.025% Tween-20, 1 mM ATP), the sample was mixed with 50 μl of 50% amylose resin pre-equilibrated in binding buffer. The mixture was incubated at 4 °C on a rotating wheel for 1.5 h, and after centrifugation (500 g at 4 °C for 2 min), the supernatant was discarded and the protein-bound resin was washed three times with 500 μl of binding buffer. After adding 25 μl of binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM maltose, the sample was centrifuged (14,000 g at 4 °C for 10 min). The supernatant was isolated by careful pipetting and centrifuged two additional times. Next, 2.5 μl of sample was applied to a freshly glow-discharged (60 s) Quantifoil R 1.2/1.3 Au 300 mesh grid, blotted for 3 s (grid 1) or 2.5 s (grid 2) at 100% humidity and 4 °C, plunge-frozen in a cryogenic mixture of liquid ethane and propane using a Vitrobot Mark IV plunger (FEI) and stored in liquid nitrogen. Cryo-EM data were collected on an FEI Titan Krios G3i system operating at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector in super-resolution counting mode. In total, 43,220 movies were acquired as two separate datasets (dataset 1, 11,964 movies of grid 1; dataset 2, 31,256 movies of grid 2) at 130,000× magnification, yielding a super-resolution pixel size of 0.325 Å. Each movie consisted of 37 subframes with a cumulative exposure of 60.059 e− Å−2 (dataset 1) or 65.580 e− Å−2 (dataset 2). EPU automated data-acquisition software for single-particle analysis (v.3.9, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was used for data acquisition, with three shots per hole and a defocus range of −1.0 to −2.4 μm in 0.2-μm increments.

Industry observers note that for both datasets, the exposures were imported to cryoSPARC live (v.4.7) for real-time processing. Datasets 1 and 2 were pre-processed separately. After patch-motion and patch-CTF correction, particles were identified using blob picker (270–290-Å diameter, elliptical blob), extracted (extraction box size: 600 pixels; Fourier-cropped to box size: 200 pixels) and classified into 100 2D classes. Next, 93,462 particles of dataset 1 and 203,735 of dataset 2 were selected for a two-class ab initio reconstruction, which resulted in a Cascade–TniQ–TnsC volume and a TnsAB tetramer volume. The Cascade–TniQ–TnsC particles were re-extracted with a bigger box size (extraction box size 1,024 pixels, Fourier-cropped to box size 256 pixels) and used for non-uniform refinement. Using a bigger box revealed additional density at the edge of the particles, corresponding to a flexible TnsAB tetramer next to the TnsC density. This volume was low-pass filtered and used to create masks for particle subtraction. After reducing the box size (extraction box size 700 pixels, Fourier-cropped to box size 350 pixels), the signal for Cascade–TniQ was subtracted from the selected set of particles and the TnsABC moiety was locally refined after aligning the volume to the centre of mass of the TnsABC mask. A 3DVA (filter resolution: 5 Å; mode: simple) yielded one reconstruction with clear density for both TnsC and TnsAB and another with a well-resolved TnsC density but only a weak TnsAB density. The volumes were used as input for two rounds of heterogeneous refinement with the initial set of particles. Next, 49,752 were assigned to the TnsAB-bound TnsC volume, re-extracted (576 pixels) and locally refined, focusing on TnsAB. To adjust the box size for the creation of a composite map, the particles were re-extracted with a larger box-size (700 pixels) and re-aligned to the centre of mass of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC mask, yielding a 49,606-particle set. An ab initio reconstruction, followed by non-uniform refinement, resulted in a Cascade–TniQ–TnsC–TnsAB consensus volume at 3.10 Å GSFSC resolution. Using the consensus map, new masks were generated for the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC, TnsC and TnsAB moieties as described above. The masks were used for particle subtraction of the TnsAB signal and local refinement of the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC complex. To improve the signal of the TnsB hooks bound to TnsC, a final particle subtraction of the Cascade–TniQ signal was followed by local refinement of TnsC. The TnsAB local refinement was repeated using the final set of 49,606 particles to match the rest of the volumes. This procedure yielded focused cryo-EM maps for the TnsAB tetramer, the hook-bound TnsC heptamer and the Cascade–TniQ–TnsC-hook complex at GSFSC resolutions of 3.36 Å, 3.30 Å and 3.09 Å, respectively. After re-alignment of the TnsAB volume, the global consensus map and the locally refined maps were combined into a composite map using the volume maximum function of ChimeraX (v.1.9). All maps and models have been deposited in the EMDB and PDB (see Data availability and Extended Data Table 3). A detailed processing workflow is shown in Extended Data Fig. 8. The QCascade–TnsC–TnsB hook model was rigid-body fitted in the cryo-EM density map using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and adjusted manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) using the above-mentioned restraints. The density corresponding to the tetrameric TnsAB was rigid-body fitted using our previously determined TnsAB PEC structure (PDB 9T7L)45. Missing regions in the protein and nucleic acid chains were built manually in Coot (v.0.9.4) with the aid of an AlphaFold3 model of TnsAB. It was not possible to determine whether the hooks bound to TnsC could be assigned to any of the TnsB copies observed in the structure, as the region between the hook and the last modelled TnsB residue (TnsB(586-604)) is disordered. It should also be noted that the 7:7 TnsC:hook observed stoichiometry probably reflects the excess of bait (His6–MBP–TnsAB) used in pull-down preparations, rather than the physiological interaction ratio, which was observed to be 7:4 in other transpososome structures6,36,41. Refinement statistics are included in Extended Data Table 3. Structure and map figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX (v.1.9) and Adobe Illustrator (v.25.4.1). The local model-to-map fit for all residues shown for the holocomplex in Figs. 1–5 is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1n–r.

#106127. Çelik pulled from Türkiye XI with left hamstring tightness as Kalulu is already out

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Juvefc ↗ Open Full Page

Çelik pulled from Türkiye XI with left hamstring tightness as Kalulu is already out

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (483 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Juvefc

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Zeki Çelik was withdrawn from Türkiye's starting line-up in Bordeaux after feeling tightness in the same left thigh muscle he injured in October.
  • Industry observers note that zeki Çelik’s international week ended before kick-off in Bordeaux.
  • In a recent development, an Emirhan Topçu own goal and a goal from Eli Junior Kroupi put France ahead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Zeki Çelik was withdrawn from Türkiye's starting line-up in Bordeaux after feeling tightness in the same left thigh muscle he injured in October. With Pierre Kalulu already sidelined, Juventus face tests that could leave them without both main right-sided defenders for Venezia and Omonia.

Industry observers note that zeki Çelik’s international week ended before kick-off in Bordeaux. The Juventus full-back was named in Türkiye’s starting line-up for Sunday’s Nations League match against France. His left hamstring tightened up as he went through the warm-up. He was taken out of the matchday squad as a precaution. Barış Alper Yılmaz started in his place.

In a recent development, an Emirhan Topçu own goal and a goal from Eli Junior Kroupi put France ahead. Abdülkerim Bardakcı scored a late reply for Türkiye. The result left France top of Nations League Group A1 with 13 points. They are through to the quarter-finals, which are due next March.

According to recent reports, çelik now returns to Turin for tests at J|Medical. Those results will decide how Juventus line up at the back after the international break.

The location is what worries Juventus. Çelik was substituted at half-time in the 2-2 Europa League draw with Rennes. His scans took place on the morning of Friday 23 October. He began a rehabilitation programme straight away and was expected back after the November break.

Tuttosport counted him among Spalletti’s first returning players, alongside Vicario and Gatti. The paper placed the Bordeaux problem in the biceps femoris of his left thigh. That is the same area as the October injury.

Industry observers note that çelik had only just returned after weeks out. That is why the warm-up incident has raised fears of a relapse. No diagnosis has yet been confirmed.

Juventus were already without Pierre Kalulu. He picked up the injury in the game against Fiorentina. He began treatment and was withdrawn from the France squad. Sky Sport Italia expected him to be out for about three weeks. That would rule him out of both the Venezia and Omonia matches.

It has been revealed that if Çelik’s problem proves to be a relapse, Spalletti could be without both of his main right-sided defenders for those two games. The schedule offers little room for recovery. The Omonia match is the second of four games in 12 days.

The league position adds pressure. After 11 rounds Juventus are seventh in Serie A with 18 points. Their record reads five wins, three draws and three defeats.

Venezia visit Turin first, at 12:30 on 22 November in round 12 of Serie A. Omonia then come to the Allianz Stadium at 21:00 on 26 November in the Europa League league phase.

#106126. Champions League contenders PSG and Bayern Munich face contrasting attacking crises ahead of crucial tests

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1060 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Champions League contenders PSG and Bayern Munich face contrasting attacking crises ahead of crucial tests

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Naim Beneddra | 25 Nov 2026 17:05.
  • Paris Saint-Germain and Bayern Munich enter Wednesday's Champions League fixtures facing significant questions about their attacking strength, with injuries forcing Luis Enrique and Vincent Kompany to reconsider how their teams operate.
  • According to recent reports, the reigning European champions host Roma without Desire Doue and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, two of the players most responsible for providing individual creativity in Luis Enrique's fluid attacking system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Naim Beneddra | 25 Nov 2026 17:05.

Paris Saint-Germain and Bayern Munich enter Wednesday's Champions League fixtures facing significant questions about their attacking strength, with injuries forcing Luis Enrique and Vincent Kompany to reconsider how their teams operate.

According to recent reports, the reigning European champions host Roma without Desire Doue and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, two of the players most responsible for providing individual creativity in Luis Enrique's fluid attacking system. Bayern, meanwhile, travel to Lille without Harry Kane, whose influence extends well beyond his remarkable goalscoring record.

Both clubs remain among the contenders for the European title, but the nature of their problems differs considerably. PSG must compensate for losing two players capable of creating advantages from wide positions, while Bayern are missing the central figure around whom much of their attacking play has been organised.

It has been revealed that their circumstances are also different in the league phase. Paris have won all four matches and collected 12 points, while Bayern sit 13th with eight points following two victories and two draws. Wednesday's matches will provide the first European examination of how both sides respond to their recent setbacks.

PSG's problems began on October 20, when Kvaratskhelia suffered an anterior cruciate ligament injury during the 4-2 victory over Barcelona. The Georgian subsequently underwent surgery, leaving Luis Enrique without one of his most effective players in one-on-one situations.

Sources indicate that the situation worsened on Saturday when Doue sustained a similar injury during the 3-2 Ligue 1 win at Nice. The France international had scored earlier in the match but was forced off before half time and now faces an extended recovery period.

The absence of both players removes two crucial sources of creativity from an attack built around movement, positional exchanges and the ability to beat defenders individually.

Industry observers note that kvaratskhelia's influence is particularly apparent on the left, where his dribbling and ability to move inside create space for overlapping teammates. Doue offers a different range of solutions, operating from the right while frequently drifting into central positions to combine with midfielders or attack the penalty area.

Losing both simultaneously could make PSG's attacking patterns easier for opponents to anticipate, particularly when facing teams prepared to defend in a compact shape.

Sources indicate that luis Enrique still has considerable resources. Ousmane Dembele is available after returning from a hamstring injury, while Maghnes Akliouche, Ferran Torres and Mika Godts provide options across the attacking line. However, finding an effective combination is likely to require more than simply replacing the two injured players with others occupying the same positions.

The Spaniard has nevertheless rejected suggestions that PSG must respond immediately in the transfer market.

It has been revealed that "We don't need to sign players in the transfer window," Luis Enrique said ahead of the Roma encounter. "It's not our style to sign a player for just six months. We're happy with our squad.".

He also emphasised the resilience his team have demonstrated in recent seasons, insisting that the injuries would not diminish their ambitions.

Wednesday's meeting with Gian Piero Gasperini's Roma presents a particularly demanding test. The Italian coach favours aggressive defending and a flexible tactical approach, potentially challenging PSG's ability to progress through central areas without relying so heavily on their absent wingers.

Gasperini acknowledged the significance of the injuries but warned against underestimating Paris.

"PSG are a proper team and can also make up for the absences of very good players with their own organisation," he stated during his pre-match press conference.

For Luis Enrique, maintaining that collective identity while introducing latest attacking combinations will be essential to PSG's hopes of challenging for a third successive European crown.

Bayern's immediate problem is concentrated through the middle of their attack, where Kane's absence has removed the team's most influential forward.

It has been revealed that the England captain suffered a syndesmosis ligament injury during Friday's 1-1 Bundesliga draw with Cologne and subsequently underwent surgery. He is expected to miss several months, depriving Kompany of a player who had already contributed 10 goals and 10 assists in 16 appearances this season.

Industry observers note that those figures illustrate the difficulty of replacing Kane. His value lies in his ability to drop into midfield, connect attacks and create space for teammates, as well as his finishing inside the penalty area.

A conventional replacement might occupy the same central position without providing the passing range and movement that allow Bayern's wide players to attack the spaces Kane creates.

Kompany's options have been further reduced by the absence of Ismael Saibari, who is recovering from an ankle injury, and Serge Gnabry. Michael Olise has also been ruled out of the Lille fixture with a foot problem, removing another significant source of creativity and attacking production.

There is some encouragement in the return of Luis Diaz, who is available again after a minor hamstring injury, while Jamal Musiala is working his way back towards full fitness. Neither development, however, eliminates the challenge of reorganising an attack that has relied heavily on Kane's contribution.

Bayern sporting director Max Eberl acknowledged that the team would need to adapt its approach.

"The dynamic of our play must change to an extent," Eberl told the club's official website. "We have to try with the team to defend well over the whole game and score the required goals.".

Kompany has similarly focused on the players available rather than those missing, describing the situation as exceptional but insisting that Bayern retain enough quality to compete.

According to recent reports, "It's a chance to get wins in a different way," the Belgian said. "Now we have to show energy and mentality.".

Unlike PSG, Bayern have less room for error in the league-phase standings. Their eight points leave them outside the top eight places that guarantee direct qualification for the last 16, making the visit to Lille important beyond its tactical implications.

According to recent reports, the two Champions League contenders therefore approach Wednesday with different priorities. PSG must preserve the variety of their wide attacking play, while Bayern need to establish a upcoming way of creating and finishing chances without Kane.

The performances against Roma and Lille will offer an early indication of which adjustments are effective, although neither match alone can establish how the injuries will shape the remainder of their European campaigns.

According to recent reports, has there been a better goalkeeper in the Premier League this season than Leeds United’s James Trafford? It is a question worth asking after his brilliance secured his side a point against Sunderland.

Opinions will vary, of course, but the body of evidence to back Trafford’s argument to permanently dislodge Jordan Pickford as England No 1 looked even stronger at the Stadium of Light.

After leaving Manchester City in the summer to play regularly following a frustrating season as backup, Trafford is proving to be a brilliant buy for Leeds. He is the most expensive British goalkeeper. More importantly, he is playing like it too.

Sources indicate that this was a tough examination for Leeds, who were not at their best, against a typically robust and physically challenging Sunderland who are getting back to doing the things that made them so difficult to play against last season. Regis Le Bris’ side created the better chances but were repeatedly denied by Trafford.

With the windy weather playing havoc, ruining the game as a spectacle, as both sides struggled for control of the ball, the two moments of quality came from Trafford in the first half.

Goalkeeping is defined by athleticism, physical strength and reflexes, but it is also about decision-making and mental fortitude. The two saves Trafford made to deny Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey in the first half were very different, but equally impressive.

In a recent development, the first was deceptively hard. Although the connection on Brobbey’s shot – back in the Sunderland side and causing chaos as usual – from the edge of the area was not the cleanest and that almost made it harder, as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the goalkeeper meant he had to watch it closely, judge the trajectory in the air and spin off the grass and still keep a strong hand, at full stretch, to push it away from danger.

The second was, arguably, even better. Trafford had come off his line as Brobbey ran into the box. He was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six-yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international. The way he kept calm, stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb, especially as an error could have led to a penalty.

Trafford may have saved with his feet, but he had cramped Brobbey for room, waited for the centre forward to make a move and timed the moment to dive at his feet perfectly. It was elite-level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

According to recent reports, trafford made two more fine stops in the second half too, both from Nilson Angulo. The first was getting down low to tip another bouncing ball wide, which had flicked off a defender too. The second punching another deflected effort away after a block had taken some of the venom out of the shot.

Sunderland will feel like they shaded the battle, but Robin Roefs also made two decent stops from long-range shots in the second half while substitute Sean Longstaff saw an injury-time effort cleared off the line.

“It’s a positive [point],” said Le Bris. “The more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.”.

“It’s a positive [point], the more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.

Sunderland were warned about “second season syndrome” and shrugged them off in the summer as they looked forward to their first European campaign for more than 50 years.

They had dismissed the gloomy pre-season predictions the previous year and had gone on to enjoy their most successful season in the top flight since the heady days of the Peter Reid era at the start of the century.

So when the “experts” told them it would be much harder this season—that they would no longer have the element of surprise and the squad would be badly stretched by the extra games in the Europa League—it was easy to ignore.

You cannot blame them. It has been a magical couple of years on Wearside where everything has gone in their favour, but reality has hit hard this season.

Sunderland are bottom of the table heading into this home game against Leeds United and have not won in the league since August.

The limp defeat at Bournemouth last weekend brought things to a head, with defender Nordi Mukiele suggesting in a post match interview that his teammates had become arrogant and had forgotten how hard they had to work last season to be successful.

There was a better performance and a decent draw away to Lech Poznan on Thursday night but Regis Le Bris’ side desperately need a win in the league.

Leeds United have been one of the story’s of the season so far and have looked dangerous in every game so far.

Sources indicate that the return to fitness of Brian Brobbey is a substantial boost for Sunderland, but I don’t think any side would like to face Leeds at the moment. The home crowd will be anxious.

Régis Le Bris has made three changes to his Sunderland side.

Brian Brobbey returns to the starting line-up after recovering from a hamstring injury, while Luke O’Nien and Nilson Angulo also come into the side.

Omar Alderete and Timur Tutierov are named among the substitutes, while Kevin Danso begins a one-match suspension following his red card at Bournemouth.

Manager Daniel Farke has made three changes to his starting line-up.

Industry observers note that jaka Bijol replaces Nico Elvedi and starts alongside Tarik Muharemovic and James Justin. Brenden Aaronson and Harry Wilson both start in place of Anton Stach and Noah Okafor, supporting Dominic Calvert-Lewin in the Leeds United attack.

Leeds United: Trafford, Justin, Bijol, Muharemović, Bogle, Ampadu, Tanaka, Gudmundsson, Wilson, Aaronson, Calvert-LewinSubs: Zetterer, Bard, Longstaff, Stach, Gruev, Cresswell, Nmecha, Okafor, Bahoya.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Sunderland and Leeds United at the Stadium of Light.

The final game of this gameweek sees these two Northern giants lock horns once again in a very intriguing encounter, with Sunderland especially in need of three points.

According to recent reports, following their opening season back in the Premier League last term, Sunderland enjoyed a historic campaign, placing seventh to qualify for European competition for the first time in 53 years. Therefore, their workload for the 2025-26 season has increased, which has caused their domestic form to suffer.

Sunderland right now find themselves bottom of the top-flight table, with just one win and four points from their opening seven league matches. They’ve lost their previous four Premier League games, but a win here could lift them out of the drop zone, depending on other results at Old Trafford and Selhurst Park.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, in the Europa League, it’s a completely different story. Regis Le Bris’ side are unbeaten, earning seven points from the first nine available. They drew 1-1 with Polish outfit Lech Poznan on Thursday evening, and given the relentless juggling act of domestic and European football, they’re already back in today against a very well-drilled team.

Leeds have made a solid start to the season and find themselves eighth in the Premier League, having only lost one match — a narrow 2-1 defeat to Arsenal at the Emirates earlier this month. Last time out, Daniel Farke’s side drew 1-1 with Manchester United at Elland Road, meaning they’re still searching for a first Premier League win since September 14.

Speaking in his preview, Farke said: “To win any point in this league, you always have to be on it. And you always have to be close to be perfect, especially for normal sides - not like the top two. And for that, we are very respectful. So we don’t go into the trap and think we are bigger than we are. We are just the second year back on Premier League level. And we fight for every point.”.

37 years after fall of Berlin Wall: How divided are Germans?

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1353 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border.
  • Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.
  • To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989, ending East Germany's isolation from the West, the event was celebrated on both sides of the border. Yet, 37 years later, many people on both sides remain deeply skeptical of each other.

Surveys show that only a minority of respondents report feeling a strong sense of community between those from former East and West Germany, and many continue to perceive significant differences.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

We asked three artists from Germany with different perspectives on the history of the country's division to share their views.

Author Lea Streisand was born in 1979 and experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall firsthand while growing up in East Berlin.

In her books and essays, she has returned to her East German upbringing many times, using literature to process it.

The novel "Hufeland, at the corner of Bötzow" (2019, Ullstein), for example, recounts the period of reunification from a child's perspective.

It has been revealed that "November 9, 1989, was simply incredible," she told DW. She was 10 years old at the time. When her mother bought her winter boots with the 100 Deutsche Marks she received from the West German state — a welcome gift given to all East German citizens — she was so disappointed that she felt like crying. But later, a friend of her parents' let her buy so many sweets at the supermarket that they lasted until Christmas.

"The disappointment really set in afterwards, with what happened over the course of the following year. It was unbelievable how quickly an entire system was suddenly swept away and a new one built up, as if to say, 'There you go. You're welcome'," Streisand recalled. "I think it was just too fast for people.".

Recent findings suggest that the people of East Germany, or the GDR, had brought about the fall of the Berlin Wall themselves through a civil rights movement and numerous demonstrations. For many, however, the goal was not to dissolve the state immediately but to reform it.

Sources indicate that among them was Anke Feuchtenberger, born in 1963 in East Berlin. Her childhood was spent in East Berlin and in the East German region of Western Pomerania, where she now lives again and feels "very much at home.".

Today, she teaches at the University of Applied Sciences in Hamburg, meaning she spends time on both sides of the former divide. Feuchtenberger is often described as Germany's most influential comic artist. Her work has also garnered international acclaim.

"Back then, as artists, we tried to bring about a change through posters and flyers — to gain more freedom without immediately abolishing socialism," she explained.

Sources indicate that at the time, the fall of the Berlin Wall stirred up mixed feelings in Feuchtenberger: "I soon realized that the creative and revolutionary aspects of our movement were very promptly being smothered by consumerism, and that nationalist tendencies — which had already been noticeable before — were coming to the fore," Feuchtenberger recalled. "That made me afraid.".

Meanwhile, for photographic artist Simon Menner, born in 1978 in Emmendingen, in the West German state of Baden-Württemberg, Berlin was very far away. As Menner put it, he experienced the fall of the Berlin Wall as a child in a "rather abstract" way. Today, Berlin is his home.

Recent findings suggest that in his experience, the way films and documentaries portrayed East Germany around the time of reunification was very bleak. "But West Germany in the '80s," he said, "was also bleak and very staid.".

This uneven portrayal of the two parts of Germany is an concern that deeply concerns Menner — partly because he unwittingly contributed to it in a small way. Among other things, Menner's work explores the topic of surveillance and how it works.

In the archives of East Germany's Ministry for State Security, or Stasi — which are freely accessible today as part of the National Archives — he discovered a massive collection of photographs that both fascinated and horrified him and which he wanted to bring to the attention of a wider public.

It has been revealed that his photo book "Top Secret" (2012, from publisher Hatje Cantz) features a selection of photos that offer a unique insight into the work of the Stasi. Some are eerie, while others are curious or even absurd.

Industry observers note that menner also tried to look into the photo archive of West Germany's Federal Intelligence Service. "I spent a year trying to gain access — without success," he said.

In hindsight, he now finds his artistic project problematic because he believes it is too one-sided, focusing exclusively on East Germany's past.

According to Menner, West Germany's intelligence services in the 1960s were not exactly models of virtue either, and he believes it is "actually high time" to critically examine this part of history as well. In his view, an honest examination of Germany's past as a whole is a prerequisite for genuine reconciliation.

Recent findings suggest that streisand believes literature can help foster mutual understanding. "Literature opens a window into experiences we haven't had ourselves," she said. "You can immerse yourself in the mind of someone who has had a different life than you have and understand what happened.".

Sources indicate that interest in these stories remains strong. In 2023, Feuchtenberger published the nearly 500-page graphic novel "Comrade Cuckoo" (published by Reprodukt), which was the first graphic novel to be nominated for the Leipzig Book Fair Prize in the fiction category.

The story spans a childhood in the fictional East German village of Pritschitanow in the 1960s in the GDR to the post-Reunification era. In it, Feuchtenberger weaves autobiographical memories of her upbringing with fantastical and fictional elements.

The artist noted she was surprised "that, so long after the fall of the wall, my stories have sparked such great interest in the West.".

In particular, the fact that the main character, Kerstin, rarely sees her parents because they both work full-time is a topic that often comes up at readings. In the GDR, everyone had the right to work, she said. At the same time, it was a civic duty.

Could the West German interest in this stem from the fact that full-time employment for both parents has long been less common in the West? It's possible, remarked Feuchtenberger.

When looking toward their shared future, the two East German women are more optimistic than Menner, from West Germany.

According to recent reports, "In Berlin, I often don't even notice anymore whether I'm in the West or the East," said Menner. "But when it comes to sociopolitical issues, politicians should listen to older and younger people more closely," he added, referring to the recent election successes of far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD . "Otherwise, things are going to get difficult in the near future.".

"It's very important to step outside our own bubble because people all over the world are facing problems. Constantly focusing on this German-German divide that has emerged between the groups doesn't help," remarked Feuchtenberger.

"For me personally, the whole problem of borders has somehow dissolved," she explained. This is due in no small part to the many trips abroad that have taken her to various places around the world.

Moreover, in her hometown near the Polish border, she observes how animals couldn't care less about the border. "They come from the east and the west and do whatever they want," she noted. That's why she also gave "Comrade Cuckoo" the working title "A German Animal in a German Forest," "because I found the absurdity of an animal having a nationality so funny.".

It has been revealed that "This East-West thing — our children won't have any interest in it at all," said Streisand. "Young people don't care where their parents come from. Can I get a job that will support a family? Do I have to go to war? Right now, completely different things are relevant.".

This article was originally written in German.

Man City's controversial orange kit sparks fan criticism as Premier League restriction emerges

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Naim Beneddra | 25 Nov 2026 17:29.
  • Manchester City's decision to wear a striking orange fourth kit during Tuesday's Champions League draw with Napoli has drawn criticism from supporter groups, while Premier League regulations mean the controversial shirt cannot be worn in domestic league matches.
  • The Citizens abandoned their traditional sky-blue colours for the 2-2 encounter at the Etihad Stadium, unveiling a special-edition strip created by Puma and Italian fashion brand C.P.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Naim Beneddra | 25 Nov 2026 17:29.

Manchester City's decision to wear a striking orange fourth kit during Tuesday's Champions League draw with Napoli has drawn criticism from supporter groups, while Premier League regulations mean the controversial shirt cannot be worn in domestic league matches.

The Citizens abandoned their traditional sky-blue colours for the 2-2 encounter at the Etihad Stadium, unveiling a special-edition strip created by Puma and Italian fashion brand C.P. Company. The launch formed part of a commercial collaboration, with the collection scheduled to go on sale worldwide on December 1.

Industry observers note that the decision proved divisive, particularly as Enzo Maresca's side extended their winless run to five matches. According to Brazilian outlet Trivela, two independent supporter organisations have questioned the timing of the initiative and its apparent prioritisation of commercial interests.

Recent findings suggest that there is also a regulatory complication. City have already registered their three regular kits for the 2026-27 Premier League campaign, meaning their latest orange design cannot be added to the selection of strips available for league fixtures.

Premier League clubs are permitted to use a maximum of three registered outfield kits during a season, normally comprising their home, away and third-choice designs.

City have already filled those places with their traditional sky-blue home strip, a black-and-yellow away kit and a predominantly white third shirt featuring blue detailing.

Their newly introduced orange shirt therefore falls outside the competition's permitted selection, regardless of whether the club wishes to use it again.

The restriction is not related to the unusual colour, the shirt's design or its association with C.P. Company. It follows from the fact that City have introduced an additional strip beyond the three registered for Premier League use.

UEFA's kit regulations operate differently, allowing clubs greater flexibility over the number of approved designs they can wear in European competition.

That explains why City were able to introduce the orange shirt against Napoli and could use it again during selected Champions League fixtures later this season.

Sources indicate that the club confirmed the arrangement in an official statement following Tuesday's match, describing the outfit as a special-edition collaboration with Puma and C.P. Firm.

Supporters will have an opportunity to purchase items from the collection at an exclusive pre-sale event at the City Store in Medlock Square on November 30, before the worldwide release the following day.

The FA Cup could also provide another opportunity to wear the shirt, although its use would require the appropriate approval from the Football Association.

In a recent development, such exceptions are not unprecedented. Arsenal received permission to wear a special white kit in the FA Cup as part of their No More Red initiative, which raises awareness of knife crime and youth violence in London.

The Premier League restriction is only one aspect of the controversy surrounding City's latest release.

According to Trivela, the Citizens Trust, an independent supporter organisation established earlier this year, criticised the decision to introduce the orange shirt and expressed opposition to initiatives perceived as explicitly promoting third-party commercial interests.

Another independent organisation, the 1894 Group, reportedly raised concerns about the club's priorities, arguing that City should be concentrating on strengthening their relationship with supporters during a difficult period.

Those objections are particularly relevant because the latest kit made its debut at the Etihad, where City would ordinarily wear their familiar sky-blue colours.

The orange design has no obvious connection to that traditional home identity. However, C.P. Company has a longstanding association with British football terrace fashion, and its partnership with City dates back to 2024.

The club therefore has a cultural and commercial rationale for the collaboration, even if some supporters remain unconvinced by its appearance on the pitch.

Tuesday's result did little to improve the mood. City were held to a 2-2 draw by Napoli despite a late equaliser from Rayan Cherki, extending a difficult run for Maresca and his players.

The manager is already facing questions about his team's performances ahead of Sunday's Premier League trip to Arsenal, making the timing of a high-profile commercial launch a particularly sensitive issue.

City have previously demonstrated that fourth kits can generate interest without provoking the same debate over their relationship with the club's identity.

Their 2024-25 special-edition shirt, developed with Noel Gallagher, celebrated the 30th anniversary of Oasis's debut album, Definitely Maybe.

Sources indicate that the design drew on the Manchester band's history and Gallagher's longstanding support for City. It was worn during Champions League fixtures against Inter Milan and Paris Saint-Germain.

The latest collaboration follows a different approach, reflecting C.P. Company's influence on football fashion rather than a specific event from the club's own history.

Sources indicate that there is no indication that City intend to withdraw the orange kit following the criticism. Their official announcement identifies it as an outfit for selected European fixtures, and the commercial launch remains scheduled for next week.

Sources indicate that for supporters attending Premier League matches, however, there will be no repeat of Tuesday's unusual appearance. City's three registered domestic kits will remain the available options, leaving the orange shirt as a feature of their European campaign.
