#106035. RANGERS 3 ABERDEEN 2: Amid all the thrills and spills, McInnes' triple switch sparks second-half revival

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1357 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dailymail ↗ Open Full Page

RANGERS 3 ABERDEEN 2: Amid all the thrills and spills, McInnes' triple switch sparks second-half revival

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1357 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 18:40 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 18:50 EST, 24 November 2026.
  • When these sides last met in the league at the end of August, Rangers were in such a dark place that you wondered if their season was already destined to be another thoroughly miserable episode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 18:40 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 18:50 EST, 24 November 2026.

When these sides last met in the league at the end of August, Rangers were in such a dark place that you wondered if their season was already destined to be another thoroughly miserable episode.

Coming just three days after going out of Europe — for the second time — to an ordinary Jablonec team, the slender win Derek McInnes’ side claimed at Pittodrie that day felt like a can being kicked down the road.

In those early weeks, the players looked lost. The manager admitted that he didn’t know what style of football he was watching. The supporters were preparing for a long, hard winter.

According to recent reports, it’s remarkable what can come from one scruffy win on the road. From that point to this, McInnes’ men have now gone 14 games unbeaten in all competitions.

Industry observers note that they have the League Cup final to look forward to next month. They are now just one point behind Celtic in the Premiership and look eminently capable of putting in a serious challenge for the title. In keeping with so many performances throughout this run, however, this wasn’t particularly convincing. Flat and rudderless for 45 minutes, Rangers were deservedly a goal behind at the interval.

Industry observers note that credit where it’s due, though. Their response at the outset of the second period was outstanding with three goals coming in 11 minutes courtesy of Ryan Naderi, Djeidi Gassama and Nico Raskin.

It has been revealed that that ought to have been the platform for many more to follow. But the performance slipped back a level. Aberdeen scored once and could easily have scored again.

Raskin (right) and Gassama celebrate after combining to put Rangers 3-1 up.

Naderi capitalises on Muller's mishandling to fire Rangers level at the start of the second half.

It was a truly thrilling match, full of slip-ups, incidents and moments of brilliance. The final stages were a tough watch for the home fans who hoped against hope that they’d see their side ease towards a routine victory.

As at Fir Park on Saturday, though, Rangers found a way and added another win to the ledger. And provided that remains the case in the coming weeks and months, none of the light blue legions will be complaining.

Despite ultimately not having quite enough to take something, Aberdeen manager Mario Frick will have been encouraged by much of what he saw here.

Had it not been for that atrocious spell at the outset of the second period, he’d have fancied his men to take something.

They certainly fashioned plenty of opportunities. It was the defensive side of the game which ultimately cost them.

McInnes drafted in Kevin Kelsy, James Penrice and Ben Godfrey with Dujon Sterling, Tuur Rommens and Kim Minsu dropping out. There was a change of shape too, with a switch to a 3-5-2. For the longest time, it did not work.

Lyons gets his head to Marshall's corner to put Aberdeen in front in the first half.

It has been revealed that while Frick kept faith with the diamond-shaped midfield which served him so well in Ayrshire, he made three changes. In came Ayoub Mouloua, Afeez Aremu and Findlay Marshall at the expense of Hicham Mahou, Ante Palaversa and Stuart Armstrong.

It has been revealed that before the game, there was a minute’s silence in memory of the late, great Ralph Brand. What a pity a couple of clowns in the visiting section were unable to keep their mouths shut for that long.

It has been revealed that rangers started brightly with Penrice’s delivery from the left causing chaos. Dan Neil had a stab at it, then Naderi. Aberdeen survived.

Once Frick’s side settled, Nicky Devlin’s cross was met by Marshall. His header was straight at Ivor Pandur.

Rangers’ general play was broken, their build-up more ponderous than patient. Gassama did manage to drop a shoulder and get a strike away but Aremu’s positioning ensured Marius Muller was untroubled.

Sources indicate that naderi was again Rangers’ most effective player, although the bar was set pretty low initially. The Czech’s lay-off invited Godfrey to let fly. His strike was well off target.

Sources indicate that while Gassama got into plenty of promising positions, his crossing continually let him down early on. On the other flank, Badredine Bouanani could not do right for doing wrong.

When the ball broke kindly to Naderi on the edge of the box, Ibrox expected the net to bulge. This time the man of the moment fired over. Rangers’ efforts in the first half were summed up by Naderi being tripped by Gavin Molloy on the edge of the box. Bouanani’s effort from the free-kick was woeful.

Aberdeen were aggressive and organised. And when the moment arose, they went forward in numbers.

McInnes shows his delight after his half-time changes helped turn the game around.

They edged in front on the half hour after Marshall won a corner which was a consequence of Frick’s men being prepared to back themselves.

According to recent reports, marshall curled the set-piece deep to the far post. Brad Lyons seemed to be invisible to those in light blue as he made a late run. Olwethu Makhanya belatedly reacted but it was too late.

Lyons got enough on his header to beat Pandur and force Raskin to make the block behind his keeper.

Recent findings suggest that the minute the scoreboard indicated that VAR were checking for a goal, you suspected the Belgian hadn’t done quite enough to keep it out. After a lengthy delay came confirmation of that fact.

How would Rangers respond up until the break? Not terribly well. Lyons’ crude foul on Gassama gave Bouanani a chance to make amends with a set-piece. This one smashed into the wall. Seconds later, the winger fired well over the top when he ought to have done better.

The Dons could easily have doubled their advantage. Jack Milne carried well and rattled the ball into Kevin Nisbet’s feet. The forward played a smart pass around the corner. Mouloua was only denied by a terrific save from Pandur.

There was still time for Mouloua to be thwarted by the outstretched leg of Makhanya as he moved to turn home a cut back.

Bluntly, it was no surprise that McInnes made three changes at the break. Off came Godfrey, Kelsy and Bouanani. On went Minsu, Rommens and Findlay Curtis. The impact was extraordinary.

In a recent development, re-energised, within 45 seconds Rangers were level. Minsu’s speculative shot did come through heavy traffic. Still, Muller had to hold it. Credit to Naderi for anticipating the fumble. The instant it bounced towards him, he instinctively lashed it home for his 10th of the season. Subdued to that point, the home fans roared their approval. And they’d rapidly be off their seats again.

As Aberdeen’s attack broke down, Naderi played a simple pass into space. Gassama had too much pace for the chasing pack. Did he have the finishing? Absolutely. What a turnaround.

Gassama squeezes his shot under Muller to put the home side ahead just after the restart.

Two goals in 90 seconds then became three in 11 second-half minutes. Gassama did superbly to motor down the left, look up and play in Raskin. The Belgian smashed the ball back across goal and in.

That should have been that. Yet three minutes later, the Dons were back within a goal of McInnes’ men. Afforded too much time on the left, Alexander Briedl picked out Marshall with his cross. Marshall swept it home with his left foot via the inside of the post.

Sources indicate that remarkably, the Dons might well have levelled. Pandur made a fine save when Minsu threatened to turn an Aberdeen corner into his own net. The ball bounced off Nisbet and just wide.

Terrific throughout, Marshall saw a good strike whistle just wide. The fact the Dons made Rangers sweat for the win will be some consolation.

Jensen Huang: Spy row, affairs leave Nvidia without its rockstar CEO

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.
  • In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier remarked Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.
  • The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.

In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier remarked Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.

The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.

Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.

The Fresh York Times first reported that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

Later Thursday, Reuters news agency alleged an intimate relationship between Huang and a second employee, citing unidentified sources.

Sources indicate that those revelations emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The woman, Alice Huang — no relation — is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.

The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.

Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.

Recent findings suggest that megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators. Huang, the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.

While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

Kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who presently works in the firm's robotics division.

Industry observers note that rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

US President Donald Trump also backed Cook on social media, writing: "A Legend replaces a Legend.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that the scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.

Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure.

Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high, however, that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the company and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race," noted Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank.

Recent findings suggest that analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole firm behind them.

His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.

Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.

Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.

Huang steered the tech giant for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.

He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang has run the company so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

At the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The manufacturer has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.

Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.

China is swiftly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.

Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.

The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.

However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.

Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.

The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

Iranian activist and Nobel Peace Prize winner Narges Mohammadi shares her story in memoir

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As PEN International marks Imprisoned Writer Day on November 15, a memoir by 2023 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi stands as a powerful act of resistance against authoritarian regimes.
  • "A Woman Never Stops Fighting — My Struggle for Freedom, Democracy and Human Rights in Iran," was recently published in German and is set to be released in English in September 2027.
  • The autobiography "portrays how Narges actually became the woman she is today — and it also reveals the price she had to pay to become that woman," Mariam Claren, spokesperson for the Narges Mohammadi Foundation Germany told DW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As PEN International marks Imprisoned Writer Day on November 15, a memoir by 2023 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi stands as a powerful act of resistance against authoritarian regimes.

"A Woman Never Stops Fighting — My Struggle for Freedom, Democracy and Human Rights in Iran," was recently published in German and is set to be released in English in September 2027.

The autobiography "portrays how Narges actually became the woman she is today — and it also reveals the price she had to pay to become that woman," Mariam Claren, spokesperson for the Narges Mohammadi Foundation Germany told DW.

Recent findings suggest that mohammadi wrote the autobiography in prison: "She was constantly writing," indicates Claren, whose own mother, activist Nahid Taghavi, shared a cell with Mohammadi for two and a half years, in Iran's notorious Evin prison. "Then, in 2020, Narges was forcibly moved to another prison. All her documents were gone. And she had to start all over.".

But she managed to rewrite it all, and her texts were smuggled out of prison in fragments by fellow prisoners and visitors who risked their own safety.

In her memoir, Mohammadi recounts pivotal moments in her life, including her childhood and youth, how she started taking action against gender discrimination, political repression, the death penalty and human rights abuses, and the personal and emotional toll of her activism.

The human rights activist has been sentenced to a combined total of more than 44 years in prison and 154 lashes. For more than a decade, she has been separated from her twin children, who are now 19 years old and live in exile in France for their own protection.

Born on April 21, 1972, in Zanjan, Iran, Narges Mohammadi became politically active while studying in physics at Imam Khomeini University of Qazvin in the 1990s.

In "A Woman Never Stops Fighting," she describes how she started mountain climbing as a student, and organized mixed-gender groups dedicated to mountaineering — a controversial initiative at the time. She also helped establish an independent student organization and advocated for political reform. Her activities led to repeated harassment and arrests by authorities.

Sources indicate that she began her journalism career in 1996, writing about Iran's student and women's movements. As her public profile grew, she became increasingly involved in Iran's civil society and human rights community.

Industry observers note that in 1998, she married political activist Taghi Rahmani. The couple's twins, Ali and Kiana, were born in 2006.

Over the course of her career, Mohammadi worked with some of Iran's most prominent human rights organizations and became a leading figure in the Defenders of Human Rights Centre, founded by 2003 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shirin Ebadi.

Industry observers note that she played a key role in initiatives promoting free elections, peace and the abolition of the death penalty, especially for juvenile offenders. She also helped establish organizations supporting political prisoners and advocating for women's rights.

It has been revealed that her first major prison sentence related to her human rights activities came in 2011. It marked the beginning of a cycle of arrests and prosecutions that would define much of her adult life.

Sources indicate that in her memoir, she describes an arrest that took place in front of her young children. At one point during her imprisonment, she lost the right to call them for several months.

She also details the brutal treatment she experienced in prison, with constant interrogations, beatings and denial of medical care.

Another central focus of her activism is denouncing the psychological effects of solitary confinement, which she had previously documented with fellow inmates in her book and documentary project "White Torture.".

Sources indicate that "When someone is subjected to physical torture, the scars, blood and infections — dreadful as they may be — serve as visible witnesses," she writes in her memoir. But, she adds, "when someone is subjected to psychological torture, no visible traces remain, and the victim cannot justify the trauma — neither to themselves nor to others. In fact, it becomes virtually impossible to even accept that one has been tortured at all, which causes the suffering to continue indefinitely.".

"This is also the goal of solitary confinement: to bring the imprisoned person to the very edge of nothingness — to strip them of their identity and of everything that makes them human," she writes.

Through her relentless campaigning against executions and state violence, she helped bring these problems to the forefront of public debate among Iranian activists.

International recognition of her work culminated in October 2023 when she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for "for her fight against the oppression of women in Iran and her fight to promote human rights and freedom for all.".

As Mohammadi was unable to attend the ceremony because she remained imprisoned in Tehran's Evin Prison, the award was accepted on her behalf by her teenage twins, who delivered her message to the world.

Following the Nobel Prize, Iranian authorities continued to pursue newly introduced legal cases against her, restrict her communications and intensify pressure on her from prison.

She became the target of a systematic smear campaign, including widespread defamation, gender-based harassment and explicit death threats.

It has been revealed that "We are firmly convinced that the Islamic Republic of Iran has deployed its cyber army — which is the second-largest, after Russia's — to this end," states Claren of the Narges Mohammadi Foundation. Conspiracy theorists even started claiming she might be working for the regime, she adds: "And what is truly terrible about this is that when a lie is repeated over and over again and spread over the course of years, it eventually leads even ordinary people to start believing it.".

In late 2024, following surgery, Mohammadi was granted a temporary medical release. Doctors warned at the time that a return to prison could seriously endanger her health.

Nevertheless, Mohammadi was brutally arrested again in December 2025, while attending a memorial ceremony for Khosrow Alikordi, a lawyer and human rights activist who died in suspicious circumstances.

In prison, she was held in solitary confinement for an extended period and her health continued to deteriorate, Claren reports. But "thanks to a public campaign, she has now been granted what is known as an interruption of detention for medical reasons.".

But "that doesn't mean she is free," adds Claren, who notes that she still suffers from serious health problems — as do many Iranians who have been tortured in prison.

In February, an Iranian court ordered additional prison sentences for Mohammadi, along with a travel ban.

Mohammadi lives in constant fear of having to return to prison any day, notes Claren, and "this all comes with the pressure to which Iranian civil society — including, of course, people like Narges — is at the moment subjected, with questions like: Will Trump launch an attack, yes or no? Will there be another war?".

Recent findings suggest that despite this uncertainty, Mohammadi continues her activism. Her international profile also helps her supporters keep addressing publicly the issue of human rights in Iran in the public eye, notes Claren: "It is incredibly important that, alongside the individual Narges Mohammadi, the focus also remains consistently on the struggle of the people in Iran for freedom, dignity, and fundamental rights — for the right to sing and dance.".

Latest Update: Could lack of money sink TFFF rainforest fund before it even rolls out?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The world's tropical forests play a vital role in slowing global heating and preserving biodiversity, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.
  • More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later logging continues.
  • In 2024, over 8 million hectares (19 million acres) of forest were lost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The world's tropical forests play a vital role in slowing global heating and preserving biodiversity, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.

More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later logging continues.

In 2024, over 8 million hectares (19 million acres) of forest were lost. And since 1990, nearly 490 million hectares of forest have been wiped out.

In a recent development, more recently, the trend has shifted in the opposite direction. Deforestation in the Amazon region of Brazil decreased by 41% from August 2025 through 2026 to reach its lowest rate since records began.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

To ensure lasting protection, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility was launched in 2025 at the COP30 climate conference in Belem, Brazil.

Because rainforests are so notable for the world, the idea behind the fund was to give money to the countries where they are located to help them preserve and protect these ecosystems.

So far, these countries have made more profit through deforestation — for example, by mining natural resources on rainforest land or farming the area.

Starting in 2027, the TFFF is expected to generate the funds needed for rainforest conservation, in part via contributions from various countries. By the end of this year, a total of $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in government capital is due to flow into the fund, mainly in the form of low-interest loans.

In addition, the TFFF is expected to issue bonds to private investors, such as banks and investment firms, to raise additional funds — initially totaling about $40 billion.

Going forward, the initiative is for governments to contribute a total of $25 billion to the pot, and for private donors to contribute $100 billion. The fund will then invest this money in international financial markets with the aim of generating profits.

Private investors who purchase TFFF bonds can expect to earn about 5% interest per bond per year, said Felix Finkbeiner, the founder of the German environmental organization Plant-for-the-Planet, where he is responsible for forest conservation and advocacy.

"Private investors' capital is very well protected," Finkbeiner mentioned, adding that any losses the TFFF might incur on the capital markets — for example, if the price of its bonds should fall — would be offset by government funds.

About 2.7% of the TFFF's profits would be set aside for countries with tropical forests.

Countries would receive $4 per year for every hectare of forest that they preserve instead of chopping down. At least 20% of these funds must be allocated to Indigenous peoples and local communities.

According to calculations by the TFFF Watch website, an independent platform released by Plant-for-the-Planet to track investments, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, would receive about $333 million for its 2024 forest stock under this system.

Finkbeiner remarked the subsidies would be paid only for intact ecosystems and not for timber plantations, with forest areas and their condition mapped and assessed using satellite imagery. Though it can sometimes be difficult to identify plantations accurately on satellite photos, he said, the technology has improved significantly over the last decade.

That means any NGO or external party with access to the satellite data can check the condition of the region, providing further oversight. If forest areas are cleared or damaged, money is deducted from the total.

Another safeguard: If countries don't use the TFFF funds for rainforest conservation, their payments could be frozen for the next few years.

The TFFF is supposed to invest, whenever possible, in government bonds issued by emerging and developing countries. Above all, the idea is not to invest in projects that harm the climate — such as those linked to oil, gas, or coal investments.

The TFFF concept has received plenty of support from environmental organizations, in part because it gives countries in the Global South significantly more sovereignty than traditional forms of development financing.

"For example, if the government of Ghana wants to protect its rainforest today, it usually asks the World Bank for financial assistance — and then the World Bank in [Washington] DC decides whether Ghana is allowed to do so," Finkbeiner remarked.

The TFFF fund is also designed to be immune to donor countries' backing out in the event of a change in government, for example. Once a contribution is made, the money remains in the fund for 40 years before being paid back.

Recent findings suggest that continuing protection is also an incentive for countries receiving money from the fund. "When a upcoming government comes into power that wants to cut back a little on climate protection, they will realize: We'll get more money if we protect the rainforest," said Finkbeiner.

For the rainforest fund to actually get off the ground, a total of $10 billion in seed capital must be raised by the end of 2026. So far, the confirmed pledges from countries, NGOs and foundations total only $7.9 billion.

Eight countries have expressed a willingness to contribute so far, including Brazil, Indonesia, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

Recent findings suggest that norway, with a pledge of $3 billion, is the largest would-be donor. However, the government in Oslo is willing to honor its commitment only if the agreed-upon total amount is in place by the end of the year.

"This deadline isn't set in stone, but otherwise the Norwegian government will have real trouble getting it through parliament," Finkbeiner mentioned.

Germany's commitment must also still be approved by the parliament. The German government has pledged about €1 billion to the TFFF starting in 2027, to be paid out over 10 years.

Other countries are also considering investing in the TFFF, including Canada, China, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.

Philanthropic organizations have pledged $88 million to the fund so far, including $73 million unveiled this week during the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Finkbeiner remains upbeat.

It has been revealed that "Promises like that always come at the last minute," he stated. "I'm very optimistic that we'll secure more commitments at the COP — and in the course of December — and that we'll then reach that $10 billion.".

Middle–Late Pleistocene Denisovans and unresolved Homo in southern China

⏱️ ~54 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, molecular and morphological evidence increasingly supports the view that most East Asian Middle to Late Pleistocene archaic Homo belong to Denisovans1, yet the presence of other contemporaneous lineages has remained unclear.
  • In a recent development, the taxonomic classification of East Asian late Middle Pleistocene and early Late Pleistocene hominins has been a subject of intense debate.
  • Sources indicate that however, morphological heterogeneity persists among these hominins, for instance, cranial capacities of approximately 1,700–1,800 ml and a Neanderthal-like temporal labyrinth configuration and/or the presence of a suprainiac fossa in Xuchang and Xujiayao, and a round orbit in Maba10,11,12.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, molecular and morphological evidence increasingly supports the view that most East Asian Middle to Late Pleistocene archaic Homo belong to Denisovans1, yet the presence of other contemporaneous lineages has remained unclear. Here we report a set of newly discovered hominin fossils (4 isolated teeth; more than 100.8 thousand years ago and 104.5–42.6 thousand years ago, respectively) from 2 cave sites (Chuanshandong and Longchuandong) in Guangxi, southern China. Integrated morphological and palaeoproteomic analyses reveal substantial phenotypic and molecular diversity consistent with at least two distinct lineages. One lineage (Longchuandong) is assigned to a Denisovan-affinity population, owing to its extreme similarity to Altai Denisovans with respect to dental morphology and single amino acid polymorphisms that match those of Denisovans from Harbin, Penghu, Bianfu Cave and Altai. The other lineage, represented by the Chuanshandong hominin, is an unresolved archaic Homo, as it carries an ancestral variant (AMELY 179M) shared with Homo antecessor and great apes and another variant (AMBN 253G) that is diagnostic of East Asian Middle Pleistocene Homo erectus but lacks the Denisovan-associated AMBN 273V variant (it being highly probable that this is inherited from H. erectus). Dental morphology in this lineage exhibits a mosaic of plesiomorphic and derived traits but no clear Denisovan affinity. These findings indicate that diverse hominin populations may have inhabited subtropical China during the Middle and Late Pleistocene, including a Denisovan-affinity population and another unresolved archaic Homo.

In a recent development, the taxonomic classification of East Asian late Middle Pleistocene and early Late Pleistocene hominins has been a subject of intense debate. These hominins are consistently characterized by plesiomorphic features, including a long and low neurocranium with a thick vault, a massive supraorbital torus, a sloping forehead and a robust mandible with a retreating symphysis, combined with derived traits such as an enlarged cranial capacity, a highly arched temporal squama, reduced prognathism and simplified dental morphology2,3,4,5. Phenotypic and molecular evidence has increasingly aligned these hominins with Denisovans2,6,7,8. For instance, the Harbin and Xujiayao crania, the Bianfu Cave radius, and the Xiahe and Penghu partial mandibles have been classified as Denisovan on the basis of palaeoproteomic and/or mitochondrial DNA analyses1,4,6,7,8,9. Phylogenetic studies based on trait matrices have linked Harbin Denisovans to Dali, Jinniushan, Hualongdong and Xiahe, suggesting a potentially broader distribution of Denisovans across mainland East Asia2.

Sources indicate that however, morphological heterogeneity persists among these hominins, for instance, cranial capacities of approximately 1,700–1,800 ml and a Neanderthal-like temporal labyrinth configuration and/or the presence of a suprainiac fossa in Xuchang and Xujiayao, and a round orbit in Maba10,11,12. Such variations have led to the proposal of distinct species, that is, pre-modern Homo sapiens, Homo juluensis and a Neanderthal-related lineage13,14,15,16,17. Moreover, most specimens attributed to the Denisovan assemblage have originated from northern and central China, with few contemporaneous hominin fossils reported from southern China, particularly subtropical regions. Thus, it remains unclear whether the East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo represent only Denisovans or multiple lineages adapted to diverse environments across a vast territory.

It has been revealed that resolution of this question requires the discovery of more hominin fossils dating to the Denisovan period, especially from regions where such remains have not yet been reported. A comprehensive comparative study centred on such fossils should be conducted, incorporating a wide range of Eurasian Homo samples to establish a robust evolutionary framework for taxonomic identification. In addition to morphological comparisons, molecular analyses are essential for accurate taxonomic assignment. However, ancient DNA preservation is poor in the warm, humid conditions of southern China, particularly for late Middle Pleistocene specimens4,18,19. In such cases, palaeoproteomic analysis offers a vital complementary approach. This technology has been successfully applied to the identification of Denisovan specimens from diverse environments (including the Xiahe partial mandible4 and rib20 from the high-altitude Tibetan Plateau; the Penghu partial mandible6 from the Taiwan strait; the Bianfu Cave partial parietal bones, radius and teeth9 from southwest China; the Xujiayao cranium and mandible1 from north China; and the Harbin cranium7 from the plain of northeast China) and the phylogenetic placement of Homo antecessor (approximately 949–772 thousand years ago (ka)) and East Asian Middle Pleistocene Homo erectus21,22.

A group of hominin fossils has been recovered from two sites in Nanning (Chuanshandong in Long’an County) and Liuzhou (Longchuandong in Luzhai County) within the karst terrain of Guangxi, a region renowned for its rich Pleistocene mammalian fossils, during surveys of late Middle Pleistocene cave deposits by our interdisciplinary team since 2016 (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). These investigations spanned an area extending more than 500 km from Chongzuo City in the southwest to Guilin City in the northeast. The discovery of these newly introduced hominin remains in this area will be critical for clarification of the geographical distribution of Denisovans and assessment of whether multiple archaic Homo lineages existed in mainland East Asia during the Middle and Late Pleistocene.

In a recent development, here we present direct U-series dating results for hominin teeth from Chuanshandong and Longchuandong (more than 100.8 ka and 104.5–42.6 ka, respectively), the optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) ages of the hominin fossil-bearing layer (between 49.5 ± 2.6 ka and 34.2 ± 4.1 ka) and a biostratigraphic chronology based on the faunal assemblage (late Middle to early Late Pleistocene age, younger than 300 ka). To determine the taxonomic affinity of the hominins, we performed detailed morphological descriptions and comprehensive metric and non-metric comparisons with a broader range of Eurasian Homo specimens. In addition, we conducted palaeoproteomic analyses of hominin teeth and compared the results with published data from H. erectus, H. antecessor, Denisovans, Neanderthals and H. sapiens to further clarify the taxonomic affinity of these new hominins. The integration of these approaches will enhance our knowledge of the diversity of the East Asian late Middle Pleistocene hominins.

Chuanshandong lies in the karst terrain of Long’an County, Guangxi (Fig. 1). Two hominin teeth and associated abundant mammalian teeth were recovered from layer 3 of an approximately 1.2-m-thick consolidated deposit adhering to the cave walls of the western chamber entrance, the bottom deposit of which was eroded (Fig. 1, Supplementary Text 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). The sedimentary sequence consisted of the following six layers, from top to bottom: yellowish-brown sand (layer 1), consolidated brown calcareous-cemented sand (layer 2), greyish-brown sandy silt (layer 3), yellowish-brown brecciated sand (layer 4), brown gravel-bearing clayey silt (level 5) and yellowish-brown gravel-bearing silt (level 6). The two hominin teeth were separated from each other by approximately 5 cm vertically and 20 cm horizontally within layer 3. The deposit in layer 3 consisted of homogeneous, fine-grained particles without lamination, with grain-size and size distributions similar to those of modern soil near the cave entrance. They were all polymodal, mostly dominated by the clay fraction with very low proportions of particles larger than 63 μm (less than 8.4%) and relatively low percentages of coarse fraction (Supplementary Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 1). This suggested that the deposit of layer 3 was derived from the modern soil outside and transported by low-energy, intermittent and short-term water activity. The hominin and mammal fossils from layer 3 were dominated by isolated teeth and may have been transported gradually into the inner cave by slope gravitation resulting from a depth gradient of approximately 5 m between the cave entrance and the burial location of the teeth. Therefore, the burial age of the fossils may substantially lag behind their true age.

Longchuandong is situated in the karst landscape of Luzhai County, Guangxi (Fig. 1). Two isolated hominin teeth and numerous faunal remains were discovered in the brownish-yellow clay (Fig. 1, Supplementary Text 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1). Given that most fossils from Longchuandong are isolated teeth, the fossils were highly likely to have been sorted and transported into the deep cave by water. No stone artefacts or other cultural relics were associated with hominin fossils at these two sites.

In a recent development, to estimate the ages of these hominin teeth, we applied both laser-ablation-based and classic isotope-dilution-based U-series dating analyses to the hominin and associated mammalian teeth (Supplementary Text 2, Supplementary Figs. 3–5 and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). The lower right third premolar (P3) from Chuanshandong yielded laser ablation U-series ages ranging from 72.2 ± 1.4 ka to 63.8 ± 1.3 ka and an isotope-dilution-based age of 62.1 ± 0.3 ka. The left P3 yielded laser ablation U-series ages ranging from 109.2 ± 2.7 ka to 97.7 ± 4.6 ka and an isotope-dilution-based U-series age of 100.8 ± 0.2 ka. These two P3s could have originated from one individual, considering their similar morphology and degree of occlusal wear (minimum number of individuals = 1). The isotope-dilution-based U-series age of 100.8 ka thus provides a minimum age for the Chuanshandong. This age was also included in the range of the laser-ablation-based U-series ages of the associated mammal teeth (211.1–37.8 ka) (Supplementary Figs. 6–8 and Supplementary Table 4). However, the OSL ages of the hominin fossil-bearing layer in Chuanshandong ranged from 49.5 ± 2.6 ka to 34.2 ± 4.1 ka; that is, they were significantly younger than the U-series ages of the hominin teeth and most mammalian fossils, suggesting slow transportation or delayed burial of these materials (Supplementary Text 3, Supplementary Fig. 9 and Supplementary Table 5).

The upper right second molar from Longchuandong (M2) yielded laser-ablation-based U-series ages of 46.9 ± 2.2 ka to 37.7 ± 2.0 ka and an isotope-dilution-based age of 42.6 ± 0.4 ka, whereas the lower right fourth premolar (P4) from the same layer returned laser ablation ages of 111.0 ± 3.6 ka to 96.7 ± 3.5 ka and an isotope-dilution-based age of 104.5 ± 0.4 ka. These ages fell within the range of the laser-ablation-based U-series ages of the associated mammal teeth (160.4–30.1 ka) (Supplementary Figs. 10 and 11 and Supplementary Table 6). Associated faunal remains from both sites represented a typical Ailuropoda-Stegodon fauna (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13). The presence of Elephas maximus and Tapirus indicus, together with the relatively small tooth size of Ailuropoda in Chuanshandong and T. indicus in Longchuandong, all indicate a late Middle to Late Pleistocene age (younger than 300 ka). Despite the limitations of each dating method, the integration of U-series, OSL and biostratigraphic context supports a Middle and Late Pleistocene age for the Chuanshandong and Longchuandong hominins.

Sources indicate that we described the dental morphology of a pair of P3s from Chuanshandong and one P4 and one M2 from Longchuandong and compared them with a broad range of Homo specimens (including H. erectus, East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo, Denisovans, Neanderthals and H. sapiens) to determine their taxonomy (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Tables 7–11). These materials occupied an intermediate morphological position between H. erectus and H. sapiens, characterized by a mosaic of dental traits and the absence of autapomorphic Neanderthal features. Nevertheless, the two assemblages exhibited distinct phenotypic profiles.

According to recent reports, the first phenotypic pattern was represented by the P4 and M2 of Longchuandong hominins. These individuals resembled the East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo with respect to both M2 and P4 morphology and exhibited notable affinity to Denisova 4 from Denisova Cave (Altai) in terms of M2 characteristics (Figs. 2 and 3, Supplementary Text 4 and Supplementary Figs. 14–17). Their P4s shared an approximately symmetrical buccal and lingual contour (unlike the mesiobuccal protruding contour typical of H. erectus and distolingual protruding contour typical of Neanderthals) and non-tapering roots (distinct from the tapering roots of H. sapiens)3,23,24 (Supplementary Fig. 17). Their M2s had comparable hypocone size, similar enamel–dentine junction (EDJ) shape and a non-dendritic EDJ surface, distinct from the tall crown topography and the absence of a hypocone or only ridge-like hypocone of H. sapiens, and from the symmetrically trapezoidal EDJ viewed occlusally and dendritic EDJ surface of H. erectus23,25,26,27,28,29,30,31 (Fig. 3, Supplementary Fig. 15 and Supplementary Table 12). The Longchuandong M2 did not exhibit clear variation compared with Neanderthals, especially in diffeomorphic surface matching analyses of EDJ shape (the typicality probabilities of being classified as Neanderthals were 42.13% and 39.11% in the between-group principal component analysis and canonical variate analysis, respectively), although Neanderthals tend to be characterized by a more skewed M2 crown viewed occlusally and a higher occurrence of transverse crest (23.5% in early and late Neanderthals)28,32 (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Table 12). In particular, the Longchuandong M2 most closely resembled Denisova 4 from Denisova Cave (Altai) when all dental features analysed were considered, including the two-dimensional crown outline shape and three-dimensional EDJ shape, in addition to the crown size, relative hypocone size and degree of elevation of the crista obliqua, which overlap among different taxonomic groups to varying degrees33,34,35 (Supplementary Figs. 15, 18 and 19).

It has been revealed that the second phenotype was represented by the paired P3s of the Chuanshandong hominin and did not align well with any established East Asian Homo member. These samples retained an erectus-like short EDJ that could be clearly distinguished from that of Neanderthals and H. sapiens and a complex root system with approximately constant root breadth from cervix to apex, which is normally found in H. erectus (for instance, the single Tomes’s root with bifurcated apex in Zhoukoudian and two-rooted pattern in Sangiran) but rarely occurs in Neanderthals or H. sapiens28,36,37,38,39 (Figs. 2 and 3, Supplementary Text 4, Supplementary Figs. 20–22 and Supplementary Table 13). However, the Chuanshandong P3s exhibited derived traits that were shared with other later Homo and distinct from those of H. erectus: reduced crown asymmetry, less pronounced distolingual protrusion, a lingually displaced polygon area, absent metaconid apex (probably sharper protoconid dentine horn) and a less crenulated mesial vertical groove on the buccal surface40,41. They were distinguishable from the East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo from Panxian Dadong, which falls within the H. sapiens range, with a slightly asymmetrical crown and tall EDJ topography, despite a non-tapering root42 (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 22).

To provide molecular evidence for taxonomy and sex attribution, we conducted ancient protein extraction on three of the hominin samples: Longchuandong M2, Longchuandong P4 and Chuanshandong right P3. After searching against the Hominidae enamel database, we removed peptides that were detected in the extraction blank or attributed to contaminant proteins to control contamination from the experiment; this resulted in 2,894, 2,038 and 2,099 identified peptides for the three samples, respectively. The endogeneity of the proteome was supported by high deamidation rates of asparagine and glutamine, as well as relatively short peptide length caused by degradation (Fig. 4). We evaluated the replicate consistency by calculating the shared and specific peptide counts between two runs of liquid chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) for each fraction from these teeth, as well as two fractions from Longchuandong P4 (Supplementary Table 14). Although more than 50% of total peptides were shared, indicating some replicate consistency, specific peptides from each run or fraction accounted for 40% or more in total; this demonstrated the necessity of conducting multiple runs or collecting multiple fractions to improve the coverage of recovered proteome. To avoid misassignment, we removed peptides matching multiple genes, and a typical enamel-specific proteome was retrieved from the three hominin samples (Supplementary Table 15). Abundant amelogenin, Y isoform (AMELY)-specific peptides indicated that all were from male individuals. We further inspected the phylogenetically informative single amino acid polymorphisms (SAPs) to determine their population assignments by validation with BLASTp, assessment of peptide depth across three software tools, evaluation of spectral quality and quantification of deamidation rates (Methods, Table 1, Supplementary Text 5, Supplementary Table 16, Supplementary Data 1 and 2 and Supplementary Figs. 23–28).

Recent findings suggest that both the Longchuandong M2 and P4 exhibited ameloblastin (AMBN) 273V (55 and 59 supporting peptides; Table 1), which is shared with East Asian Middle Pleistocene H. erectus, Harbin, Penghu, Bianfu Cave, Denisova 25 and Denisova 3, and with some H. sapiens from Southeast Asia and Oceania with high levels of Denisovan introgression6,9,22,43,44,45. In phylogenetic analysis, the two Longchuandong samples were grouped with Denisova 3 with 100% support (Supplementary Text 6 and Supplementary Fig. 29). Given the age of the samples and the morphological similarity between the Longchuandong M2 and Denisova 4 from Altai Denisova Cave, the Longchuandong samples are likely to represent a Denisovan-affinity lineage in south China.

Unlike the two Longchuandong samples, Chuanshandong carried a SAP, AMBN 253G, supported by nine peptides (Table 1), among which seven peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) had a complete series of y- and b-ions surrounding the SAP. This SAP has been reported in three groups of late H. erectus from Zhoukoudian, Hexian and Sunjiadong22, but all other comparative specimens in Hominidae present AMBN 253A, including H. antecessor from Atapuerca21, H. erectus from Dmanisi21, Harbin7, Penghu6, Bianfu Cave9, TNH2-1 from Laos46, Denisova 3 (ref. 43), Denisova 25 (ref. 45), 9 Neanderthals47,48,49,50,51,52, Ust’-Ishim53, H. sapiens and non-human great apes. In addition, AMELY 179M, an ancestral variant that is shared with H. antecessor21 and non-human great apes but not with H. sapiens, Neanderthals or the Denisovan clade, was also identified in Chuanshandong with seven supporting peptides (Table 1); among these, two PSMs had two b-ions bracketing the SAP, and eight PSMs had one b-ion when the SAP was located at the amino terminus. Phylogenetic analysis indicated that Chuanshandong formed a sister group to the common ancestors of Neanderthals, Denisovans and H. sapiens (posterior probability: 100%; Supplementary Fig. 29). The integrated evidence indicates that Chuanshandong may belong to a lineage distinct from the Denisovan in mainland southern China.

The scarcity of hominin fossils from subtropical southern China during the Middle to Late Pleistocene transition has hampered our understanding of the geographical distribution of Denisovans and the potential existence of other Homo lineages in mainland East Asia. Here we report 4 isolated hominin teeth from Guangxi (Chuanshandong and Longchuandong), dated to at least 100.8 ka and 104.5–42.6 ka, respectively. These ages establish the specimens as contemporaries of northern Denisovans (approximately 300–45 ka)4,7,8,20,54,55 that provide crucial fossil evidence of non-sapiens Homo in subtropical regions adjacent to southeast Asia during this interval. Although both the Chuanshandong and Longchuandong hominins exhibited a mosaic of plesiomorphic and derived traits, palaeoproteomic analysis revealed variations in AMBN 253 and 273, as well in as AMELY 179, which allowed phylogenetic placement of these samples. The results indicate that at least two non-sapiens Homo populations may have existed in southern China’s subtropics during the Middle and Late Pleistocene.

Industry observers note that among these diverse populations, the Longchuandong materials provide compelling evidence for the presence of a Denisovan-affinity population in subtropical southern China. Compared with H. erectus and H. sapiens, the Longchuandong more closely resembled other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo, Altai Denisova 4 and Neanderthals with respect to M2 morphology but could be differentiated from Neanderthals by its P4 features. These two specimens carried the AMBN 273V variant found in Harbin, Penghu, Bianfu Cave and Altai Denisovans, whereas Neanderthals and most H. sapiens carry the AMBN 273M variant6,7,9,43,44,47,48,49,53. These integrated morphological and molecular data together support the identification of Denisovan-affinity populations in subtropical southern China. In previous enamel proteomic studies, AMBN 273 was found to be polymorphic in Denisovans, with the M variant in Laos TNH2-1, M/V in Denisova 25 and Harbin, and V in Longchuandong, Penghu, Bianfu Cave and Denisova 3 (refs. 6,9,22,43,45,46), indicating regional variation of molecular characteristics within this lineage. Taking the Longchuandong finding into account, there is evidence that Denisovans were distributed in Siberia, northern China, the Tibetan Plateau, the Taiwan Strait, subtropical southern China and tropical Laos, suggesting their possible adaptability to diverse environments, from cold and arid high-altitude plateaus to hot and humid low-altitude regions4,6,7,8,9,20,46,56,57. Neanderthals have not been discovered in regions with confirmed Denisovan distribution other than Siberia. Given their widely separated geographical regions, the morphological similarity between Longchuandong Denisovans and Neanderthals (for instance, with respect to M2) does not necessarily indicate hybridization. Instead, it may simply reflect the limited diagnostic value of certain anatomical features in distinguishing these two taxa. Unlike the similarity in M2 morphology, Denisovans and Neanderthals can be effectively differentiated by other dental traits, such as the crown shape of P4 and M1, the labial convexity and tuberculum dentale of I1, and other cranial and mandibular traits1.

It has been revealed that in contrast to Longchuandong, the remains from Chuanshandong were marked by an ancestral variant (AMELY 179M) shared with H. antecessor and great apes and another variant (AMBN 253G) shared with East Asian Middle Pleistocene H. erectus but absent from contemporaneous Denisovans, Neanderthals and H. sapiens. In addition, Chuanshandong retained a plesiomorphic short crown and complex roots, differing notably from Neanderthals, H. sapiens and the Panxian Dadong (which is considered to be potentially Denisovan on the basis of broader dental comparisons with other East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo)42. Although Chuanshandong differed from East Asian H. erectus in having more progressive dental features and in the presence of AMBN 273M, the fact that they shared AMBN 253G implies that they may be related. The presence of an ancestral variant (AMELY 179M) and an erectus-like variant (AMBN 253G) suggests that the Chuanshandong hominin belongs to a primitive Homo lineage that may have survived into the Late Pleistocene in a geographical refugium. Admixture among existing archaic Homo in southern China or gene flow from H. erectus are plausible explanations for the unique molecular and morphological attributes of Chuanshandong hominin.

According to recent reports, the findings of this study show that the subtropical area in southern China may have hosted multiple populations of archaic Homo during the Middle and Late Pleistocene. In addition to the previously suggested Neanderthal-related hominin at Maba in the adjacent Guangdong Province16,17,58, we have now identified both a Denisovan-affinity hominin and another unresolved non-sapiens archaic Homo in this region. However, such phylogenetic inference based on the limited proteomic data is preliminary. More molecular data accumulated in the future, spanning broad geographical regions and time periods, and including ancient DNA from these archaic hominins, will provide us with a better understanding of the taxonomic value of specific proteomic mutations or variants and their variability between archaic and modern populations. Moreover, key diagnostic characteristics, especially trait combinations that significantly vary among different taxa, should be systematically screened from the relatively rich morphological dataset to define a lineage. Finally, it will be crucial to propose possible interpretations that can account for both morphological diversity and molecular variability, to further illustrate the framework of human evolution in East Asia.

According to recent reports, A sliding calliper was used to measure the mesiodistal and buccolingual dimensions of the hominin teeth, with recordings taken to the nearest 0.1 mm. We applied the terminology and grading criteria of the Arizona State University Dental Anthropology System59, as well as the standards of Martinón-Torres et al.28, to describe and score crown characteristics, including the hypocone size, the crista obliqua, the transverse crest of the upper molar and the transverse crest of the lower premolar. Root structures of lower premolars were scored using Wood’s system60. The Chuanshandong and Longchuandong hominins were compared mainly with East Asian late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo or Denisovans, East Asian/Southeast Asian H. erectus, Homo heidelbergensis, early and late Neanderthals and H. sapiens.

According to recent reports, to quantify the crown contour shape, cusp and fovea arrangement, and main occlusal groove orientation of the M2 and P3, we conducted two-dimensional geometric morphometric analyses on the basis of occlusal photographs of the teeth oriented in anatomical position following the procedure introduced in refs. 32,40. All specimens were digitally mirrored to the same antimeres as the Chuanshandong and Longchuandong specimens in Adobe Photoshop 12.0 when they were from the opposite side. Before semilandmark placement, the interproximal wear facet was digitally restored to its original state according to the extent of wear and the profile of the neighbouring contour.

Recent findings suggest that for the P3 analysis, four landmarks were placed at the anterior fovea, posterior fovea, protoconid apex and metaconid apex. Forty equidistant semilandmarks were defined along the crown contour. For the M2, three landmarks were placed at the intersections of the buccal and central grooves with each other and with the crown contour. These landmarks delineated four distinct curves along the crown contour and in the occlusal grooves. Each of them was divided into different and equidistant segments, and the dividing points were designated as semilandmarks. In total, 3 landmarks and 36 semilandmarks were defined on the occlusal surface of M2.

In a recent development, landmark and semilandmark coordinates were digitized using TpsDig2 v.2.12 (https://www.sbmorphometrics.org/soft-dataacq.html)61. Procrustes superimposition (minimizing Procrustes distances) was performed on the raw coordinates using the geomorph package (v.3.5)62. Principal component analysis was then conducted on the resulting shape variables. The ggplot package (v.4.0.3)63 was used to produce a scatter plot of principal component 1 against principal component 2 for visualization of morphological variation among different taxonomic groups.

Sources indicate that the teeth from Chuanshandong and Longchuandong were scanned using the Phoenix V|tome|x M microfocus CT cabinet system at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. The scanning parameters were as follows: 160 kV, 120 μA, isotropic voxel size of 34.20 µm, 0.2-mm-thick copper filter. Microcomputed tomography data of Neanderthals from Krapina were downloaded from the NESPOS database64. Tomographic slices in TIFF format were imported into Mimics v.17.0 (Materialise, https://www.materialise.com) for segmentation of enamel and dentine and virtual reconstruction of the pulp cavity. The resulting EDJ was exported in STL format for subsequent shape analysis. The worn dentine horn apices of Longchuandong M2 and Chuanshandong P3s were restored by two observers independently following a geometric method validated in previous studies in Avizo v.9.2 (https://www.thermofisher.com/amira-avizo)65 (Supplementary Fig. 30).

Industry observers note that the three-dimensional EDJ models were imported into Avizo 9.2, and all specimens were superimposed using the ‘Align Surface’ function. Following superimposition, the STL files were saved and converted into VTK format using ParaView v.5.6.0 (https://www.paraview.org/). The VTK files were then read into Deformetrica v.4.3 (https://gitlab.com/icm-institute/aramislab/deformetrica) for quantification of deformations among the EDJ surfaces, modelled as diffeomorphisms66. Control points and momenta encoding the deformation parameters were generated and imported into R v.4.1.0 (https://www.r-project.org/)67. Principal component analysis, between-group principal component analysis and canonical variate analysis were performed using the following packages: RToolsForDeformetrica v.0.1 (ref. 68), ade4 v.1.7-17 (ref. 69), Morpho v.2.8 (ref. 70), gtools v.3.9.5 (ref. 71) and freesurferformats v.0.1.15 (ref. 72). Two sets of EDJ, independently reconstructed by two authors, were also analysed, and the results were compared to provide an indication of the reliability of the virtual reconstructions of the worn dentine horns (Supplementary Fig. 31).

Six samples were collected from the fossil-bearing layer of the Chuanshandong section, as well as two samples from the modern soil near the cave entrance, for grain-size analysis. Bulk samples were first treated with 30% hydrogen peroxide to remove organic matter, followed by 10% hydrochloric acid to remove carbonates. Subsequently, the samples were dispersed with 0.5 N sodium hexametaphosphate. Grain-size was measured using a Malvern Mastersizer 3000 particle analyser with an analytical precision of less than 1%.

Industry observers note that high-resolution U-series in situ analysis using laser ablation system coupled with multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (LA–MC-ICP-MS) was conducted to directly date the Chuanshandong and Longchuandong hominin teeth. Laser ablation was performed using an NWRimageGEO high-energy laser ablation system (Elemental Scientific Lasers), and mass spectrometry was performed with a Neoma MC-ICP-MS system (Thermo Scientific). A high-precision MC-ICP-MS U-series dating method using solution nebulization after chromatographic separation was also applied to hominin teeth as an accuracy test. Integration of both procedures provided a minimum age for the hominins at Chuanshandong and Longchuandong. Laser-ablation-based U-series analyses were also conducted on freshly cut cross-sections of associated mammalian teeth recovered from the same stratigraphic layer within a 1-m radius of the hominin teeth (Chuanshandong). These analyses were carried out at Nanjing Normal University and the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, using the LA–MC-ICP-MS methods described in ref. 73 and the solution method described in ref. 74.

The age of the hominin teeth from Chuanshandong was constrained by optical dating of the hominin fossil-bearing sediments. Three sediment samples were collected using stainless steel tubes (20 cm long, with a diameter of 5 cm) hammered horizontally into a freshly dug vertical stratigraphic section. The tubes were immediately sealed with aluminium foil, wrapped with black plastic bags and taped to prevent light exposure and moisture loss. Sediment from the light-exposed end of each tube was separated and used for dose rate measurements, and material from the middle was used for equivalent dose (De) measurements. Sample preparation followed standard procedures described previously75. Coarse-grained quartz (90 μm to 150 μm) was extracted for De measurements.

Recent findings suggest that luminescence measurements were performed on a Risø Model DA-20 TL/OSL reader equipped with a 90Sr/90Y beta source for irradiation76 and an EMI 9235QA photomultiplier tube. Blue light-emitting diode stimulation (470 ± 30 nm) was used at 90% of 50 mW cm−2 full power, and 7.5 mm Hoya U-340 filters (transmission between 290 nm and 370 nm) were used for the quartz OSL measurements. The single-aliquot regenerative-dose protocol was used to determine the De (refs. 77,78) (Supplementary Table 17).

The uranium, thorium and potassium concentrations of the three samples were measured by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry and used to calculate the environmental dose rate. In situ water content (moist mass/dry mass) was determined by weighing samples before and after drying and assigned an absolute uncertainty of ±5%. Elemental concentrations were converted into an effective dose rate using the revised dose rate conversion factors79 and water content attenuation factors80. The cosmic dose contribution was estimated on the basis of the burial depth of the sample, the thickness of the overlying cave roof (approximately 30 m), the zenith-angle dependence of cosmic rays, and the latitude, longitude and altitude of the site81. Final dose rates and deposition ages were calculated using DRAC82. Details of sample preparation, measurement and data analysis are provided in Supplementary Text 3.

Industry observers note that microinvasive acid etching was conducted on the tooth enamel for protein extraction, using an approach modified from a published protocol83. After cleaning with a disposable toothbrush, the tooth was wrapped with parafilm with the small etching region exposed. Then, the etching region was washed with 3% hydrogen peroxide for 30 s and rinsed with ultrapure water. We conducted an initial etch of 2 min by placing the etching region on to the 5% (v/v) hydrochloric acid solution in the cap of a 1.5-ml microcentrifuge tube. This etch solution was discarded. Then, a second etch of 15 min was performed twice in the cap of another microcentrifuge tube, and the etch solutions were combined. After desalting with C18 ZipTips (Thermo Fisher Scientific), the peptides were eluted into 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid in 80% acetonitrile. The eluted solution was further vacuum-evaporated before being subjected to LC–MS/MS analysis.

Industry observers note that A Neolithic human tooth from the Xiawanggang Site (approximately 5 ka) in Henan Province, China, was chosen as a positive control sample (referred to as ‘Xiawanggang’). The positive control sample and a blank extraction (negative control sample) were processed in the same batch as the hominin samples with the same protocol. All sample treatments were performed in the dedicated clean room for ancient protein analysis in the Molecular Paleontology Laboratory at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences. To evaluate the replicate consistency and improve the coverage of recovered proteome, we etched two spots on Longchuandong P4 and obtained two fractions. Two LC–MS/MS runs were conducted for each fraction from these teeth.

Industry observers note that the eluted peptides were analysed in data-dependent acquisition mode on an Orbitrap Exploris 480 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) interfaced with an Easy n-LC 1200 HPLC system (Thermo Scientific) at the Central Laboratory, Capital Medical University, Beijing, China. A trap column (100 μm i.d. × 2 cm, C18) and analytical column (150 μm i.d. × 15 cm, C18) were used, both packed in-house with 3 μm reversed-phase silica (Reprosil-Pur C18 AQ, Dr. Maisch GmbH). Mobile phase A was 0.1% formic acid in water, and mobile phase B was 0.1% formic acid in 80% acetonitrile. The peptides were separated using a 125-min linear gradient program (0–1 min, 1–9% B; 1–101 min, 9–28% B; 101–113 min, 28–42% B; 113–117 min, 42–99% B; 117–125 min, 99% B) at a flow rate of 350 nl min−1. For the mass spectrometry, full scans were measured with a m/z range from 350 to 1,500, a resolution of 60,000, an AGC target of 300% and a maximum injection time of 50 ms. The precursors were selected for higher-energy collisional dissociation fragmentation with an isolation window of 1.6 m/z and a dynamic exclusion of 60 s. MS2 scans were obtained with a resolution of 15,000, a normalized collision energy of 30%, an AGC target of 75% and a maximum injection time of 22 ms.

All the raw data files from the hominin samples, as well as those from the positive and negative control samples, were searched using PEAKS Online (v.11.5)84, MaxQuant (v.2.6.0.0)85 and pFind (v.3.2.2)86. Multiple rounds of target database searching were supplemented with searching of a contaminant database used in a previous publication7.

First, the data were searched against the entire human reference proteome downloaded from UniProt (proteome ID UP000005640, accessed on 20 May 2022) using PEAKS Online, including peptide de novo, PEAKS DB, PTM and SPIDER. The precursor ion mass tolerance and fragment ion mass tolerance were set to 10 ppm and 0.02 Da, respectively. Unspecific digestion was chosen. Deamidation (NQ), oxidation (M), hydroxylation (P), phosphorylation (STY), pyro-Glu from E and pyro-Glu from Q were set as variable modifications, and a maximum of three modifications were allowed for each peptide. The peptide length was set from 6 to 45. A false discovery rate of 1% at the spectral level was used to filter the results. Proteins were accepted if at least two peptides were present. Main enamel proteins were identified in the hominin samples, whereas no dentine-related collagens were detected. This was not unexpected, because the acid etch approach can only extract proteins from the superficial enamel and cannot access deeper layers such as dentine. Thus, dentine collagens were excluded from further analysis.

A second round of database searching was conducted using three software tools against a custom-built database, referred to as the ‘Hominidae enamel database’ in this study. This database was composed of sequences for 12 main enamel proteins: amelogenin, X isoform (AMELX), AMELY, AMBN, enamelin (ENAM), amelotin (AMTN), odontogenic ameloblast-associated protein (ODAM), matrix metalloproteinase 20 (MMP20), kallikrein 4 (KLK4), tuftelin (TUFT1), collagen α1(XVII) chain (COL17A1), albumin (ALB) and α2-HS-glycoprotein (AHSG). Species were restricted to Hominidae, including archaic hominins such as Denisovans and Neanderthals. Protein sequences, including canonical and isoform sequences, were downloaded from UniProt and obtained from the translated Hominid Palaeoproteomic Reference Dataset available at Zenodo87. Previously published protein sequences from extinct archaic hominins (H. antecessor, H. erectus, Penghu)6,21,22, Paranthropus88 and Gigantopithecus89 were also incorporated. The parameters for data searching on PEAKS Online were the same as those used in the initial search against the entire human reference proteome. The parameters for MaxQuant and pFind were similar, with a few adjustments: for MaxQuant, phosphorylation (STY) was excluded from the variable modifications, the PSM and protein false discovery rates were set to 1% and 10%, respectively, and the ion tolerance and maximum number of modifications for each peptide were set to default values; and for pFind, hydroxylation (K) was also set as a variable modification, and open search was enabled. The possible mutations identified by PEAKS SPIDER and pFind open search were added to the original database for iterative data search and validation.

After removal of peptides detected in the negative control sample or assigned to contaminant proteins, we used the remaining peptides from each hominin and positive control sample to calculate deamidation profiles to support their endogeneity90.

It has been revealed that after excluding SAPs that were supported by a single peptide or indistinguishable owing to post-translational modifications7, we manually checked the variants within the Homo genus that met initial thresholds (PSM count ≥ 2, PSM ratio ≥ 10% and intensity ratio ≥ 10%) to confirm their reliability6,7,88. The criteria were as follows.

Industry observers note that BLASTp: first, all the supporting peptides were submitted to BLASTp search against the NCBInr database. Peptides that also matched proteins from other genes or from some archaeal, bacterial or fungal species were removed from further evaluation and calculation.

Depth across different software: after BLAST filtration, variants were retained for further consideration only if each software tool retained at least two peptides.

MS2 support: we manually inspected the MS2 spectra of all supporting PSMs to confirm the presence of y- and b-ions around the SAP. Two levels of criteria were applied: ‘MS2 support’ required at least one y- or b-ion linked to the SAP, whereas ‘strict MS2 support’ required at least two y-ions or two b-ions bracketing the SAP. An exception was made for terminal SAPs, for which a single associated ion was accepted for the strict classification. The number of peptides meeting each criterion was then calculated.

It has been revealed that deamidation rate: using peptides containing asparagine or glutamine residues, we calculated deamidation levels on the basis of spectral count and ion intensity. The number of PSMs and total count of covered N and Q sites were also recorded. An elevated deamidation rate in these peptides suggested an endogenous origin, which reinforced the reliability of the SAP identification.

Using these criteria, we evaluated eight positions across the three hominin samples (Supplementary Data 2) and confidently identified four of them. One of these was AMELY 59M, a male-specific SAP commonly used for sex identification83; details of the other three reliable SAPs are shown in Table 1.

We combined the overlapping results from the three software tools and used them to generate consensus sequences for each protein from the three hominin samples with Biopython (v.1.83)91. For sites with more than two amino acid variants, we calculated the number of PSMs, the PSM ratio and the intensity ratio for each variant. In PEAKS Online and MaxQuant, a variant was considered to be reliable if it met all of the following thresholds: PSM count ≥ 2, PSM ratio ≥ 10% and intensity ratio ≥ 10% (ref. 7). In pFind, the intensity ratio was discarded. Confident heterozygous positions were identified as those for which multiple amino acid variants passed these filters. On the basis of the overlapping results from the three tools, no heterozygous positions were retained in the three hominin samples. Amino acid variants supported by a single peptide were excluded. The unreliable phylogenetically informative SAPs inspected above were also marked as ‘X’ in the consensus sequences. Finally, the consensus sequences of six proteins, AMELX, AMELY, AMBN, ENAM, COL17A1 and ALB, were reconstructed.

The comparative dataset contained four archaic individuals, five extant great ape species, a gibbon (Nomascus leucogenys) and a macaque (Macaca mulatta). The protein sequences of four archaic individuals were obtained from the Hominid Palaeoproteomic Reference Dataset87; these individuals comprised Denisova 3, Altai Neanderthal, Chagyrskaya 8 and Vindija33.19. Protein sequences for extant great apes and other primates were retrieved from UniProt and NCBI (Supplementary Table 18). The six proteins were aligned using MAFFT (v.7.490)92 and concatenated with R package phylotools (v.0.2.2; https://github.com/helixcn/phylotools), resulting in a dataset with a total length of 4,108 amino acid positions. We also detected 16.67%, 14.51% and 14.68% non-missing sites in Longchuandong M2, Longchuandong P4 and Chuanshandong P3, respectively. Leucines were converted into isoleucines, as these two amino acids are isobaric and were indistinguishable in the tandem mass spectrometry used in this study.

We performed phylogenetic analysis on the aligned dataset using MrBayes (v.3.2.6)93. The best partitioning schemes and substitution models were chosen using PartitionFinder (v.2.1.1)94. Two Markov chain Monte Carlo runs were performed for 10,000,000 generations, with sampling every 5,000 generations. Convergence was evaluated using the average standard deviation of split frequencies and log likelihood values. Effective sample sizes were checked using TRACER (v.1.6)95. After 25% burn-in, effective sample size values for all parameters were greater than 200, indicating sufficient sampling. Then, a 50% majority-rule consensus tree was constructed, with clade frequencies representing posterior probabilities.
